articles.title: Humanlike AI May Strengthen Women’s Agreement With Sexist Stereotypes
articles.authors: Sterling Williams-Ceci; Rachel Minkowitz; Lior Zalmanson; Michael MACY; Mor Naaman
articles.abstract: AI can influence societally-consequential attitudes by generating biased arguments – but can it influence our attitudes without changing its arguments at all? In four experiments (N = 2,762), we show that the mere presence of humanlike features in an AI chatbot influences women to more strongly accept ideologically-compatible sexist stereotypes, biases that often resist influence and have societal harm. This influence operates indirectly by increasing “mind perception” – the belief that AI is conscious and thinking – which increases perceptions of its trustworthiness. Our contribution is that anthropomorphism’s influence extends beyond increased trust toward AI itself, impacting women’s broader attitudes about their competence and status. This influence happens when women are attentive during conversations with AI. As developers add more anthropomorphic features to AI, the harms of stereotypes it repeats will increase for vulnerable groups – but making AI appear less humanlike can mitigate this risk.

articles.title: Culturally Prompted Large Language Models Remain Anchored to Western Values
articles.authors: Zhao Wang; Yilin Xu; Joshua Conrad Jackson
articles.abstract: One proposed solution for reducing cultural bias in large language models (LLMs) involves “cultural prompting,” in which LLMs are explicitly instructed to respond on behalf of a cultural group. However, past studies have yielded inconsistent claims about the efficacy of cultural prompting. Here we test whether these inconsistent findings can be explained through an anchoring and adjusting account, whereby cultural prompting moves LLM responses away from a default representation anchored in wealthy Western values, but this adjustment is insufficient. We test this account by prompting three commercial LLMs to answer 117 items from the World Values Survey on behalf of 66 countries. We then compare their responses with data from 97,220 humans. Consistent with our predictions, we find that cultural prompting moves LLMs closer to human responses, but the shift is insufficient, particularly for poorer and culturally distant countries. Culturally prompted LLM responses remained more secular and emancipative than human responses. We also find that the biases of culturally prompted models were clustered by cultural heritage. Countries in closer geographic proximity and with more similar religious profiles showed similar patterns of misrepresentation. In addition to these results, we find a surprising pattern for Western countries in which cultural prompting makes responses more secular and emancipative than the model’s default representations. Many of our findings are broadly consistent with an anchoring and adjustment account, but this account cannot fully explain why cultural prompting leads models to overshoot human means for Western countries.

articles.title: Canonical Correlation Analysis of Multidimensional Perfectionism and Mental Health Among Filipino Young Adults
articles.authors: Renz Louis T. Montano
articles.abstract: Perfectionism is a multidimensional personality trait that has been consistently linked to both negative and positive mental health outcomes. Yet recent research has increasingly reduced perfectionism to broad higher-order factors leaving specific dimensions underexamined. The present study examined how the six dimensions of Multidimensional Perfectionism according to Frost et al. (1990)—Concern over Mistakes, Doubts about Actions, Personal Standards, Organization, Parental Expectations, and Parental Criticism—relate to positive and negative mental health outcomes among Filipino young adults. Canonical correlation analysis was employed in a sample of 1,093 participants (Mage = 22.10, SD = 1.66) to capture the multivariate patterning of associations between perfectionism dimensions and four mental health indicators: stress, anxiety, depression, and life satisfaction. Two significant canonical functions emerged. The first function (Rc = .649, 42.1% shared variance between the two canonical variates) linked Concern over Mistakes, Doubts about Actions, Parental Criticism, Parental Expectations and Personal Standards to higher stress, anxiety, and depression, and lower life satisfaction. The second (Rc = .332, 11.0% shared variance between the two canonical variates) linked Personal Standards and Organization to greater life satisfaction and lower depression, with weaker associations with anxiety and stress. These findings highlight the value of examining individual perfectionism dimensions rather than broad higher-order factors. Parental dimensions, in particular, appear especially relevant in the Filipino context.

articles.title: Factor Structure and Convergent Validity of the Scale of Perfectionism and Excellencism (SCOPE) Among Filipino Licensure Examination Reviewees
articles.authors: Renz Louis T. Montano; Jan Patrick G. Gutierrez
articles.abstract: The Model of Excellencism and Perfectionism (MEP) distinguishes between striving for high yet attainable standards (i.e., excellencism) and the pursuit of rigid, inflexible ones (i.e., perfectionism). The current study examines the psychometric validity of the Scale of Perfectionism and Excellencism (SCOPE) among two samples of Filipino adults preparing for a licensure examination. Results from confirmatory factor analyses supported the two factor structure of the SCOPE. Convergent validity was supported through expected cross-sectional associations with the Frost Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale as well as time-lagged associations with subjective well-being. Time 1 excellencism was positively associated with Time 2 life satisfaction and positive affect, whereas Time 1 perfectionism was positively linked with Time 2 negative affect. Overall, these findings provide support for the validity of the SCOPE and the assumptions of the MEP, suggesting that pursuing excellencism—rather than perfectionism—is associated with greater well-being during intense career preparation.

articles.title: An emic way of examining morality based on Moral Foundations Theory: development and validation of the Moral Foundations Patterns Questionnaire in Japan
articles.authors: Hideya Sanada; Yoshito Tan; Haruki Oka
articles.abstract: How should morality be measured in a cross-cultural context? Although Moral Foundations Theory combines etic (universal) and emic (local) concepts, existing measures are largely etic. Therefore, we proposed an emic approach for measuring etic constructs of MFT, introduced a new construct, Moral Foundations Patterns, and developed the Moral Foundations Patterns Questionnaire (MFPQ) in Japan. We conducted five studies to develop and validate the MFPQ (total N = 2,161), using two different sampling platforms to diversify sample characteristics. We showed MFPQ has adequate reliability and validity. Finally, we discussed how this emic MFPQ can be applied in cross-cultural research and argued that MFPQ can contribute to the stringent tests of the Moral Foundations Theory's key claims and support cross-cultural comparisons of its construct.

articles.title: Maternal Childhood Experiences and Mother–Infant Bonding: A Longitudinal Path Analysis of Perinatal Mental Health and Psychosocial Resources
articles.authors: Ana Rabasa Serrano; Sandra Doval; Alejandro de Miguel Álvaro; Maria Laura Quintanilla Cobián; Marta Giménez-Dasí
articles.abstract: Maternal childhood experiences may shape perinatal mental health and mother–infant bonding (MIB). This longitudinal study examined pathways linking adverse (ACEs) and benevolent childhood experiences (BCEs) to MIB through pregnancy adaptation and postpartum mental health, considering resilience and social support. We followed 404 pregnant women to 3 months postpartum. Path analyses showed that higher ACEs were associated with poorer pregnancy adaptation (β = .108, p = .020), which predicted greater postpartum depressive symptoms and poorer MIB. Social support and resilience protected against prenatal maladjustment and postpartum depression, while social support buffered the association between pregnancy adaptation difficulties and depressive symptoms (β = −.104, p = .006). BCEs were associated with better pregnancy adaptation through psychosocial resources. The model showed excellent fit (CFI = 1.000, RMSEA = .000) and explained 23.6% of MIB variance. Similar patterns emerged for anxiety. Findings highlight indirect pathways and the protective role of psychosocial resources.

articles.title: Is virtual reality beneficial and for which outcomes? Comparing VR and 2D in higher education classroom learning
articles.authors: Mikko Haavisto; Johannes Halttu; Tomi Jaakkola
articles.abstract: The transition from hands-on experience to computer-aided design poses challenges for students’ understanding of 3D structures because traditional 2D computer screens limit spatial perception. Immersive virtual reality (VR) offers a potential solution but its effectiveness and feasibility compared to 2D screens in a classroom context are unclear. This experiment investigates to what extent VR affects learning, motivational, and perceived outcomes, and cognitive load compared to 2D screen environments in dental technology education. It also examines how individual differences, such as spatial ability and VR proficiency, influence these outcomes. First- and second-year dental technology students (n = 45) participated in a preregistered within-subject crossover experiment. Because participants had more than a thousand times more prior experience with conventional 2D screens than with VR, the intervention started with VR orientation lessons. Participants then studied framework partial dentures and dental bridges once in VR and once in a 2D screen environment. Data from pre- and posttests were analyzed with mixed-effects models to account for repeated measurements and individual differences. The results showed that VR increased presence/immersion, interest/enjoyment, and perceived competence, and produced a small nonsignificant advantage in 3D comprehension. In contrast, 2D screen learning led to higher factual knowledge performance and lower total cognitive load. Individual differences explained a large portion of variance in outcomes. The benefits of VR were mostly experiential and motivational, whereas 2D screens supported better factual learning with lower total cognitive load. Classroom VR may therefore be useful as an addition to conventional instruction.

articles.title: Context Sensitivity Underlies Emotional Intelligence and Flexible Emotion Regulation in Daily Life
articles.authors: Riley Leckie; Carolyn MacCann
articles.abstract: The effectiveness of emotion regulation strategies depends on situation factors, such that effective emotion regulation involves regulatory flexibility (flexibly matching the regulation strategies you use to the context you are in). Recent research shows that two emotional intelligence abilities (emotion understanding and management) predict regulatory flexibility. This connection is assumed to be based on individual differences in context sensitivity (which underpin both emotional intelligence and regulatory flexibility). The current pre-registered study tests this assumption, aiming to replicate the emotional intelligence/regulatory flexibility link while adding a novel measure of context sensitivity in daily life. Participants (N = 131) completed baseline assessments of emotional intelligence and up to 30 experience sampling surveys (n = 2,901) across five days. Surveys measured four emotion regulation strategies and five appraisals of emotionally relevant situational features. Variability in strategies and appraisals was used to derive regulatory flexibility and context sensitivity metrics both in each situation (between-strategy and between-appraisal variability) and across situations (within-strategy and within-appraisal variability). All prior effects linking emotional intelligence to regulatory flexibility were replicated and there were two new findings. First, both emotional intelligence abilities predicted higher context sensitivity in each situation (between-appraisal variability), but not across situations (within-appraisal variability). Second, higher context sensitivity predicted higher regulatory flexibility at both the within-person and between-person level. These findings support the assumption that context sensitivity underlies both emotional intelligence and regulatory flexibility. To refine proposed measures of context sensitivity in daily life, future research should look to disentangle general appraisals of pronounced changes in the objective characteristics of the world from sensitivity to more nuanced changes.

articles.title: Synchronised group singing enhances social bonding more than group conversation or recitation does: A Registered Report across 30 languages
articles.authors: Zixuan Jia; Yuto Ozaki; Danya Vivianne Pavlovich; jiawen huang; Emmanouil Benetos; Uswatun Khasanah; Sasha Calhoun; Gakuto Chiba; Yoichi Kitayama; Shinya Fujii
articles.abstract: The evolution of music, language, and prosociality has been debated since before Darwin. The social bonding hypothesis proposes that these phenomena may be interlinked: musicality may have facilitated the evolution of social bonding beyond the possibilities of spoken language. Although dozens of experimental studies have argued that synchronised rhythms can promote bonding, methodological issues including publication bias, sample bias, experimenter effects, and appropriateness of experimental controls make it unclear whether synchronous singing reliably and generally enhances bonding relative to speaking. Following a peer-reviewed Stage 1 Registered Report protocol, we collected data from randomized controlled in-person experiments with 1,017 participants singing and speaking in groups of 5-10 in 30 diverse languages (N = 901 participants after planned quality control exclusions). Our results strongly supported all three of our pre-registered confirmatory hypotheses (all Bayes Factors > 30): (i) synchronised group singing enhances self-reported social bonding (20.9% mean increase), a significantly greater increase than (ii) group conversation (12.9% increase) or (iii) synchronous recitation (15.2% increase). Unregistered exploratory analyses suggested that perceived synchronisation and enjoyment are key predictors of social bonding, results are not artefacts of expectancy or group size, and singing’s bonding effects may be stronger in non-Western than Western contexts. Group singing may serve as a better bonding activity than speaking activities in settings such as school or workplace orientation events. Our study provides strong cross-cultural empirical evidence that music is not merely “auditory cheesecake” that is “useless” compared with language (Pinker, 1997). All forms of vocal communication increase social bonding, but group singing bonds us together over 1.5 times more on average than spoken conversation does.

articles.title: Developing Effective GenAI Users: The Missing Motivational System and Why It Matters for Equity
articles.authors: Kali Trzesniewski; Sarah J Gripshover; Allison Master
articles.abstract: Research on Generative AI (GenAI) in education has largely focused on how much students use it and its impact on learning. This framing overlooks the motivational processes driving students’ choices. We propose broadening research to include the study of what cultures, contexts, and learning experiences give students the knowledge, skills, beliefs, and motivation to become effective GenAI users. We define effective GenAI use and propose a motivational model of how learning environments and students' perceptions of them shape their goals and GenAI engagement choices, with attention to educational inequities that may emerge.

articles.title: Two Wisdoms, Two Pathways to Well-Being: Locus of Control among Tribal and Non-Tribal Youth in Jharkhand
articles.authors: Manoj Kumar Mallick
articles.abstract: Background: Locus of control is widely treated as a near-universal predictor of psychological well-being. Most supporting evidence comes from Western, individualist samples. Whether this link holds equally in indigenous Indian communities remains unclear. Objective: This study compared locus of control and psychological well-being between tribal (Adivasi) and non-tribal youth in Jharkhand, India, and tested whether community moderates the strength of the relationship between the two. Method: A cross-sectional comparative design was used with 500 youth (250 tribal, 250 non-tribal), stratified equally by employment status and gender. Participants completed a 24-item locus of control scale and Ryff's six-dimension Psychological Well-Being scale. Results: Non-tribal youth scored substantially higher than tribal youth on both locus of control, t(449.4) = 23.76, p < .001, d = 2.12, and psychological well-being, t(326.2) = 13.83, p < .001, d = 1.24, with the largest subscale gap on Environmental Mastery, d = 2.09. The correlation between locus of control and well-being was far stronger among non-tribal youth (r = .93) than tribal youth (r = .43), a difference confirmed by a Fisher z-test, z = 13.08, p < .001. Conclusion: Community identity shapes not only mean levels of agency and well-being but also how tightly the two are linked, suggesting tribal well-being draws on pathways beyond individual perceived control.

articles.title: Sensitivity to Prosody at 6 Months Predicts Vocabulary at 24 Months
articles.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Alejandrina Cristia; Amanda Seidl
articles.abstract: Children’s language acquisition appears effortless, and advances enormously between the first word period, at about 12 months, to the stage at which complete and often complex sentences are produced, at about 3 years. However, this apparently miraculous process may in fact rely on knowledge that the child has began to accumulate even before birth. Indeed, work on infant speech perception in the last 40 years suggests that infants begin to attune to their native language during the first year of life.

articles.title: Ethical Considerations Around Surveillance Technologies for Suicide Prevention in Public Places: Bringing Together Staff and Lived/Living Experience Perspectives
articles.authors: Bethany Cliffe; Ian Marsh; Alex Dark; Andy Willis; Penny Phillips; Laura Joyner; Lisa Marzano; Keith Hawton; Carlisle George; Peter Craig
articles.abstract: This research brings together lived/living experience and professional stakeholder perspectives to explore ethical considerations around the use of surveillance technologies for suicide prevention in public places. The study employed qualitative interviews with people who have lived/living experience, focus groups with professional stakeholders, online ethnography of suicide discussion forums, and ethnography at public sites which have high rates of suicides. Framework analysis was used to interpret the interview and focus group data, which was then triangulated with ethnography notes to develop three themes: 1) Expectations around surveillance in public; 2) Experiences of surveillance: balancing harms with saving lives, and 3) Human response matters: experiences of intervention. Our findings show that surveillance technologies are typically associated more so with criminality than suicide, which can lead to anxieties around possible consequences of their use for suicide prevention. We also identified tensions between the pressures on staff to prevent suicides, through using surveillance technologies for example, versus the risk of causing harm in the process. Additionally, surveillance may detect someone in distress, but the prevention comes from the human intervention, which needs to prioritise empathy, retaining autonomy and ongoing care to support the individual. A key conclusion from this work is that surveillance technologies do not operate in isolation and so the broader context and systems should be considered to ensure that suicide prevention is done so in ways that are ethical and that aim to reduce harm.

articles.title: What are we measuring when we measure moral concern?
articles.authors: Matti Wilks; Bastian Jaeger; Paul Bloom
articles.abstract: Understanding the factors that shape who we consider worthy of moral concern has become a focus of moral psychology. This research generally shows that we care most about our family and close others, and less about non-humans and the environment. However, these studies sometimes yield unusual or nonsensical results. We demonstrate that these findings can be somewhat explained by issues with the conceptualization and measurement of moral concern. Study 1 reveals that many studies do not define their construct. Study 2 demonstrates weak convergent validity among five existing measures of moral concern. Study 3 highlights that laypeople actively differentiate between facets of moral concern, granting greater rights to a murderer than an apple tree, while expressing greater care and compassion for a tree. These findings indicate that treating distinct constructs, such as rights, obligations, and care, as interchangeable may limit our measurement and understanding of moral concern.

articles.title: The psychological burden of “mild” aphasia: Greater associations with psychosocial well-being than with language severity
articles.authors: Deborah Levy; Kent Meinert; Katelyn Urena; Julianne M Alexander; Davida Fromm; Brian MacWhinney; Brielle C Stark
articles.abstract:
Objectives: Depression is common following stroke and neural injury, and individuals who develop aphasia—a language disorder—face an increased risk. However, people with aphasia are rarely assessed, referred, or treated for post-injury depression, an issue that may be further exacerbated in mild cases that lead to direct discharge home. Here, we examined the prevalence and correlates of depression in a cohort characterized, on average, by very mild or “latent” aphasia.  

Methods: Using the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) and the Western Aphasia Battery (WAB), we investigated relationships between depression and aphasia in 79 individuals with and 73 individuals without aphasia. Subgroup analyses investigated (a) sentiment in response to the open-ended question “How do you think your speech is these days?” and (b) self-reported psychosocial quality of life (Stroke Aphasia Quality of Life; SAQOL-39). 

Results: Individuals with aphasia showed higher rates of depression than neurologically healthy peers. Depression severity did not relate to aphasia severity. However, depression severity did relate to (a) the emotional valence of participants’ descriptions of their speech, (b) younger age, and (c) poorer psychosocial quality of life.  

Conclusions: These findings indicate that depressive symptoms are elevated even among individuals with very mild aphasia, and are more closely associated with younger age, negative valence about speech, and poorer psychosocial quality of life than with objectively measured aphasia severity. This underscores the importance of assessing the lived impact of communication changes across the full spectrum of post-injury aphasia.

articles.title: Implementing an evidence-based 'identification-to-intervention' approach through school Mental Health Support Teams: A qualitative study of expected implementation determinants
articles.authors: Alice Rose Phillips; Rosie Underhill; Michael Larkin; Cathy Creswell; Rachel McGuire; Hollie Edwards; Catherine Gallop; Ian MacDonald; Falko Sniehotta; Tessa Reardon
articles.abstract:
Background: Anxiety disorders are highly prevalent in childhood and are associated with academic and social difficulties. Although effective early interventions exist, many children do not access support due to complex referral routes and limited-service provision. ‘Identification-to-intervention’ (i2i) approaches address these barriers by combining universal screening with a targeted therapist-guided parent-led online intervention. In England, Mental Health Support Teams (MHSTs) deliver evidence-based interventions in schools so may be well-placed to implement i2i approaches. We lack understanding of factors which might influence implementation of i2i for child anxiety problems in a routine practice context. 

Method: Semi-structured interviews were conducted with MHST staff (n=16), primary school staff (n=6), and parents/carers (n=6) across England. Interviews were guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR 2.0)’s implementation determinants and analysed using template analysis. 

Findings: i2i was viewed as a simplified and accessible route to early mental health support. Participants identified barriers to parents/carers accessing i2i, including stigma-related concerns, literacy or language challenges, and limited familiarity with MHSTs. MHST staff felt i2i aligned with their remit and current skillset. Although some school and MHST staff viewed i2i as timesaving, others anticipated workload increases. Usual referral and clinical data management systems would need adjustment to allow direct contact from parents and the collection of screening data. 

Conclusions: i2i approaches are considered acceptable and appropriate across parents/carers, school staff and MHSTs, but structural barriers associated with MHSTs would need to be addressed to optimise implementation.

articles.title: Experienced vs. actual gaze reciprocity in repeated social interactions: A gateway toward social connectedness
articles.authors: Julian Gutzeit; Luise Hölting; Antonia Sophie van Duijn; Lynn Huestegge
articles.abstract: In many contexts, direct gaze is regarded as a socially rewarding signal that promotes positive interpersonal evaluations, yet most evidence stems from single, in-the-moment judgments of briefly presented faces. Across three eye-tracking experiments, we examined whether repeated gaze-contingent interactions shape more enduring social evaluations. Participants repeatedly exchanged gaze with a few on-screen virtual partners who reciprocated their gaze with systematically different probabilities. Afterwards, participants estimated gaze reciprocity rates for each partner and completed several ratings (e.g., feelings of social connectedness, social agency). Notably, participants reliably distinguished between gaze reciprocity rates of interaction partners even when differences in actual gaze reciprocity were small and close to chance (40% vs. 60%), though estimates were compressed toward the middle of the range. Critically, while objective gaze reciprocity rates showed little consistent relation to social evaluations, subjectively perceived reciprocity rates were robustly associated with social connectedness and social agency across experiments. Additionally, some experiments pointed to associations with likability and trust (entrusted money in an economic Trust Game). However, these associations did not extend to implicit behavioral measures (free-choice gaze selection, gaze cueing). A pooled multilevel mediation analysis confirmed that objective gaze reciprocity rates predicted connectedness indirectly, via subjective perception. Together, these findings suggest that social evaluation is shaped more by the experience of being looked at than by objective gaze reciprocity itself, at least when gaze reciprocity levels are somewhat difficult to differentiate.

articles.title: How observers decode pain from facial reactions. Distributed patterns of facial muscle contractions drive pain judgments in both naturalistic and synthetic expressions.
articles.authors: Nurefşan Üzmez; Ilaria Mirlisenna; Daniele Pugliese; Giada Dirupo; Laura Riontino; Corrado Corradi-Dell'Acqua
articles.abstract: Assessing others' pain relies heavily on facial expressions, yet how individuals translate observable facial features into pain judgements remains poorly understood. We combined a retrospective analysis of naturalistic spontaneous pain expressions across three different cohorts (Study 1, N = 398) with a reverse correlation experiment using synthetic facial stimuli (Study 2, N = 63), to investigate which facial muscle contractions (Action Units, AUs) drive pain judgments. Across both studies, we consistently found brow lowering (AU 4), nose wrinkling (AU 9) and brow raising (AU 1/2) as key contributors, alongside a more variable role of mouth movements. Multivariate pattern analysis indicated that pain judgments rely on a distributed set of facial AUs, rather than on single diagnostic cues. Finally, tailored co-engagement analysis from Study 2 identified AU pairs that, when combined, facilitate (AUs 1 + 12, AUs 4 + 24) or inhibit (AUs 4 + 9) pain assessments. Neither participants' own sex, the sex of the displayed face, nor participants' empathy traits substantially influenced pain judgments. These findings provide a first systematic mapping of the observable facial muscle contractions that drive human pain decoding. The identified facial features are best interpretable in terms of multiple, partly independent patterns of facial response, rather than a single prototypical template of pain expression.

articles.title: The Long Shadow of the Wall: Socialization Signatures in Public-Events Knowledge Across East and West Germany
articles.authors: Ulrich Schroeders; Priscilla Achaa-Amankwaa; Oliver Wilhelm
articles.abstract: Germany’s division and subsequent reunification provide a rare historical possibility to examine how regionally segregated information environments are reflected in what people know and how long such differences persist. In a national sample of 1,012 German adults aged 30–80 years, participants completed a 120-item multiple-choice test of public-events knowledge spanning 1960–2019, including items specifically targeting East- and West-German events from the pre-1990 period. While overall knowledge levels were similar among East- and West-socialized respondents, the item-level differences were pronounced, especially for East-specific items in pop culture, arts and literature. Nested cross-validated elastic-net models yielded near-perfect discrimination between East and West socialization in older cohorts (ages 51–80; AUCs > .96), slightly lower discrimination among ages 41–50 (AUC = .93), and a sharp drop in the youngest cohort (ages 30–40; AUC = .67). East-specific items contributed most strongly to classification, which is consistent with the concept of cultural hegemony and an asymmetric information flow. Despite post-1990 convergence, persistent geographic patterns in knowledge profiles remain. Public-events knowledge thus carries a cohort-dependent socialization signature, leaving detectable traces of historical division even after societal convergence.

articles.title: Infant-directed songs as a source of language input: Do infants segment words from playsongs?
articles.authors: Arina Shandala; Eniko Ladanyi; Mridula Sharma; Natalie Boll-Avetisyan
articles.abstract: Singing is an important communicative feature in caregiver-infant interaction that potentially provides infants with linguistic information. Nonetheless, little is known about how infants process words in songs. Therefore, the present study investigated infants’ ability to segment words from playsongs. German-learning 8-9- and 11-12-month-olds (n = 67, 43% female, 57% male) were familiarized with playsongs containing repetitions of a pseudoword. Subsequently, their word recognition was tested by measuring their looking behavior while listening to spoken familiar and novel pseudowords. Results revealed a significant listening preference for novel over familiar pseudowords in 11-12-month-olds, indicating their ability to segment pseudowords encountered in playsongs (β = -0.14, p = .014). In 8-9-month-olds, no group-level evidence for a preference was detected. Exploratory analyses of music-related questionnaires revealed no links with task performance. Our results provide the first findings that by their first birthday, infants are able to segment words from playsongs, a song genre whose value for learning is commonly assumed but has rarely been studied empirically.

articles.title: Affective Framing of Environmental News Headlines Influences Engagement, Donations, and Memory
articles.authors: Alyssa Hannah Sinclair; Danielle Cosme; Jose Carreras Tartak; Emily B. Falk
articles.abstract: Negativity captures attention and motivates people to read and share news, but can also harm mental health and sometimes discourage action to address long-term problems like climate change. Negative affect also has complex effects on memory—for example, focal details may be enhanced, but peripheral details can be distorted or forgotten, leaving individuals vulnerable to future misinformation. Here, we investigated an alternate route to increasing engagement with news: evoking positive affect by emphasizing opportunity and progress toward future goals. In two experiments, we adapted environmental news headlines to feature different aspects of each story, emphasizing Crisis or Opportunity. Both Crisis and Opportunity framing (and negative and positive affect, respectively) motivated reading and sharing, relative to the unaltered headlines. Crucially, consistent with theoretical predictions, we identified a trade-off: Crisis framing had the strongest effects on immediate engagement (increasing sharing and real charitable donations), but impaired memory for peripheral details; in contrast, Opportunity framing enhanced memory for news content. In a third study, we investigated real-world engagement with news about climate change by computationally classifying content in >25,000 news headlines on social media; Opportunity and Crisis framing were both associated with increased likes, reposts, and replies. Overall, we demonstrate that the affective framing of news modulates reading, sharing, donations, and memory in laboratory and real-world settings.

articles.title: What Race Means for Health among Black Americans: How Microaggressions Shape Self-Efficacy and Readiness for Behavior Change
articles.authors: Amanda Almond
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Objectives: Persistent racial disparities in cardiovascular health among Black Americans reflect not only structural inequities in the United States, but also the racialized meanings of cardiovascular disease reproduced through public and private health communication. Drawing on ecological systems theory, this research examines how beliefs linking race and cardiovascular disease are reinforced through routine clinical interactions and how these meanings shape health behavior change. Method: Across two experimental mixed-methods studies, a model integrating ecological, social–cognitive, and behavior-change frameworks was tested. In Study 1 (N = 374), health-message framing was experimentally manipulated to examine effects on self-efficacy and decisional balance while controlling for prior experiences of racial microaggression in medical contexts. Study 2 (N = 589) extended this work by testing whether conceptualizations of race as biological/genetic and social/political moderated these effects. A subset of participants (n = 57) voluntarily provided narratives of racially charged healthcare experiences, which were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis to contextualize quantitative findings. Results: Racial microaggressions from health professionals disrupted self-efficacy and decisional balance for cardiovascular health behaviors. Endorsement of biological versus social race beliefs moderated these effects, shaping both their magnitude and direction. Qualitative findings revealed how everyday clinical interactions reproduce racialized meanings of disease risk and personal control. Conclusions: These findings identify clinical communication as a consequential site where racial meanings of disease are constructed and psychologically internalized, influencing motivation for health behavior change. Addressing biologically essentialist framing in healthcare may therefore be critical for strengthening self-regulation and reducing cardiovascular disparities among Black Americans.

Keywords: racial microaggressions; health communication; self-efficacy; decisional balance; Transtheoretical Model; ecological systems theory; racial essentialism; cardiovascular health disparities

Public significance statement: How health professionals and public campaigns talk about race matters for behavior change. This research shows that subtle racialized cues in medicine can weaken Black patients’ sense of control and readiness to take preventive action. Training clinicians to avoid biological essentialist framing may improve patient engagement and help reduce cardiovascular health disparities.

articles.title: Brain and Muscular Signatures of Local and Global Temporal Dynamics in Facial Expressions
articles.authors: Rafal Marcin Skiba; Patrik Vuilleumier
articles.abstract: Natural facial expressions are inherently dynamic events governed by precise temporal coordination between facial features, yet the neurobiological mechanisms integrating kinematic timing, facial mimicry, and emotional evaluation remain poorly understood. Here, we combined event-related fMRI with simultaneous continuous facial electromyography (EMG; corrugator supercilii and zygomaticus major) and behavioral psychophysics in 27 healthy adult participants to examine how temporal global synchrony versus analytic asynchrony (8% and 18% onset lags between upper and lower facial features) across two dynamic speeds (1.5 and 3 sec.) shapes emotional processing. Naturally unfolding synchronous expressions distinctively engaged bilateral primary motor cortices, supplementary motor area (SMA), and primary somatosensory cortex. In contrast, kinematically disrupted expressions preferentially recruited the right posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS), fusiform gyrus, and inferior frontal gyrus (IFG). Parametric modulation analyses revealed a clear dissociation between somatic and cognitive tracking: trial-by-trial facial muscle mimicry engaged a distributed sensorimotor simulation network that severely fractured or collapsed during asynchronous kinematics. Conversely, subjective intensity evaluations of unnatural asynchronous expressions triggered an extensive recruitment of the bilateral amygdala and the entire longitudinal axis of the right STS, pointing to heightened computational demands for resolving perceptual ambiguity and social conflict. These findings demonstrate that natural temporal synchrony is a prerequisite for automatic motor-affective embodiment, whereas kinematic temporal disruptions shift processing toward lateral social-perceptual networks to analytically resolve fragmented communicative signals.

articles.title: Social prioritization of others can be explained by representational  closeness to the self
articles.authors: Meike Scheller; Georgios Velimachitis; Gabrielle Foster; Greesha Yadav
articles.abstract: Visual cognition is shaped not only by sensory input, but also by social relevance. While self-related information is processed preferentially, similar advantages extend to close others. How prioritization rapidly extends to others, however, remains unclear. We propose a framework of ‘representational closeness’, whereby individuals cognitively represented closer to the self, benefit from more efficient processing. Devising three markers – closeness, boundary imprecision, overlap – in a reanalysis of Scheller & Sui (2022, n = 43) and a new experiment (n = 78), we show that this framework explains processing benefits across two domains: friends over strangers, and more over less attractive strangers. Faster and more accurate responses, reduced response variability, and increased self-other confusion tracked representational closeness. These findings suggest that prioritization reflects a general organising principle of social perception through which cognitive resources are dynamically allocated according to social relevance, linking visual processing to the structure of social representation.

articles.title: Beyond the control bottleneck: cognitive control reconfigures its neural and computational architecture to meet task demands
articles.authors: Riccardo; Francisco Barcelo; Giovanni Pezzulo
articles.abstract: Cognitive control enables flexible adaptation of behavior, but it has associated costs: task rules must be held in memory and updated when they change. It remains unclear whether these costs arise from a unitary control bottleneck or from the interaction of multiple computational processes, and how such processes are implemented in the brain. Here we recast rule maintenance and switching within a computational model based on probabilistic (active) inference, which we apply to trial-by-trial behavioral and EEG data from a cued task-switching paradigm. Behavior showed a speed–accuracy dissociation, with slower responses during rule repetition and reduced accuracy during rule switching. We identified three separable model parameters as necessary to explain behavior: context stability, cue sensitivity and action precision. These parameters were dynamically reweighted across task contexts, with context stability predominating during rule maintenance and cue sensitivity during rule updating. They also influenced behavior through dissociable routes: higher action precision selectively improved accuracy without slowing responses. Using hierarchical Parametric Empirical Bayes with out-of-sample cross-validation, we related these latent parameters to electrophysiological signals, revealing both context-invariant and context-specific mappings: parietal P3b latency tracked cue sensitivity across conditions, whereas frontal beta latency and the frontal P3a indexed context stability in a context-dependent way. The neural implementation of context stability reorganized with task demands, shifting from frontal beta during switching to frontal theta during maintenance. Together, these findings move beyond the bottleneck view, suggesting that cognitive control is best understood as an adaptive computational architecture that integrates endogenous and exogenous information while reconfiguring its neural implementation according to task demands.

articles.title: Inconclusive mediated effect of adverse childhood experiences on suicide risk among depressed adolescents: A reanalysis of Ye et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix published by Ye et al., we reexamined the evidence underlying their proposed mediation model linking adverse childhood experiences to suicide risk in adolescents with depression. We show that the observed associations can be reproduced almost exactly by a different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional assumptions advanced in the original study. Within this alternative framework, self-reported adverse childhood experiences, anhedonia, self-hate, and suicide risk are treated as observable manifestations of a broader construct reflecting core self-evaluation. The results illustrate the challenge of model underdetermination in observational research, whereby competing theoretical accounts may provide equally good representations of the same data. These findings suggest that alternative model specifications should be considered and that correlational evidence alone offers limited support for specific influencing mechanisms.

articles.title: If you try hard but still fail to help, regulating others’ emotions will take an emotional toll
articles.authors: Zachariah Yung Weeks; Hester Xiao; Carolyn MacCann
articles.abstract: Existing evidence conflicts as to whether trying to regulate another person’s emotions is depleting (makes the regulator feel worse) or replenishing (makes the regulator feel better). Research suggests that different mechanisms produce different effects for the regulator: greater regulatory effort predicts higher negative affect, whereas greater perceived efficacy predicts lower negative affect. However, research has not yet tested how effort and efficacy combine to influence regulator outcomes. The current studies test whether the regulator’s positive and negative affect are predicted by: 1) their regulatory effort, 2) their perceived regulation efficacy, and 3) the effort-by-efficacy interaction. Study 1 (N = 119) used experience sampling (5 days, 30 occasions), and Study 2 (N = 120) used twice-daily reports over 10 work days. Multi-level models clustered occasions within persons. Across both studies: 1) effort predicted greater negative affect at both within- and between-person levels; 2) efficacy predicted less negative affect at both within- and between-person levels and greater positive affect at the within-person level; and 3) there was a significant effort-by-efficacy interaction on negative affect at the between-person level only (effort predicted greater negative affect more strongly at lower perceived efficacy). Results demonstrate that the costs of regulating others’ emotions are due to effort and the benefits are due to perceived efficacy which has practical implications for contexts that require sustained regulation of others (such as family carers and healthcare roles). Future research should use experimental designs to investigate causality.

articles.title: A longitudinal investigation of Germany’s 2025 general election: Implications for system-legitimacy, governmental (dis)trust, and electoral trust
articles.authors: Evan A. Valdes; Rosalind Searle; James H Liu; Cornelia Sindermann
articles.abstract: This registered study examined whether Germany’s 2025 general election shaped system-legitimizing beliefs and governmental (dis)trust, and whether electoral trust moderated these responses over time. Using multiply imputed data from a three-wave online longitudinal panel (N = 518; 1,554 observations), we found that system-legitimizing beliefs increased immediately after the election results were announced but were no longer reliably elevated one month later. More right-leaning respondents reported stronger system-legitimizing beliefs overall, although ideology did not reliably predict change over time. Governmental (dis)trust showed a more politically asymmetric pattern: trust increased among respondents more aligned with the election’s rightward direction, but distrust increased among those less aligned. Electoral trust was associated with stronger system legitimacy and greater governmental trust overall, but did not consistently buffer post-election reactions. At the final wave, higher electoral trust amplified ideological divergence in governmental (dis)trust, including increased distrust among left-leaning respondents. Exploratory party-based analyses further indicated that alignment with the election outcome in a multiparty system depended not only on ideology, but also on party support, coalition participation, and control over governing authority. These findings show that elections can produce distinct system-level and government-specific responses in complex multiparty contexts.

articles.title: Maintenance Orientation in Top-Down Political Communication Increases Pro-Environmental Policy Support
articles.authors: Yael Ecker; Joris Lammers
articles.abstract: Despite overwhelming evidence of the consequences of climate change, many voters—in particular conservatives—oppose pro-environmental policies. Research shows that this opposition can be overcome by reframing the issue in ways that appeal to conservatives’ motives. An important limitation to this literature is that it relies heavily on artificial stimuli in controlled settings, leaving open whether the framing of real political communication shapes conservatives' support for climate action. To address this gap, we examine natural variation in how climate change is framed in top-down political communication across the political spectrum. Drawing on the ternary goal model, we distinguish between progress, maintenance, and protection as three fundamental goals that guide climate action. We propose that maintenance-oriented messaging—reflecting a desire to maintain valued current states—is more effective in increasing conservative political support for climate action. To test this, we use a multilingual machine learning model to rate the goal orientations of pro-environmental policy statements from party platforms across four democracies and then testing voters’ support of these statements. We find that conservatives’ support for pro-environmental statements increases with the degree of maintenance orientation in the text (β = 0.27, p < .001). Moderately strong (+1SD vs -1SD) maintenance orientation reduced the liberal-conservative gap by 31%. In contrast, the degree of progress or protection orientation did not affect conservatives’ support. These findings confirm the importance of policy framing in the debate about climate change and support the practical relevance of maintenance frames to increase conservative support for climate action.

articles.title: “Suicide is cringe!”: Content analysis of 46,071 mental health videos from adolescents’ TikTok feeds
articles.authors: Rebecca Godard; Amber van der Wal; Ine Beyens
articles.abstract: Adolescents frequently watch videos related to mental health on TikTok. Despite significant risks (e.g., pro-suicide/self-harm messages) and opportunities (e.g., helpful resources, social support) posed, there has not yet been a large-scale, comprehensive investigation of this content. To address this gap in the literature, we used data donations to identify 46,071 TikTok videos about mental health viewed by 102 Dutch adolescents over a five-year period. Using a combination of supervised automated and manual content analysis approaches, we described the topics, content presentation styles, and creators of these videos. Videos were primarily related to mental health symptoms and experiences (e.g., anxiety and depressive symptoms) and mental health disorders (e.g., autism, depression, eating disorders), with a smaller number discussing positive aspects of mental health (e.g., recovery, coping) and mental health treatment. Videos predominantly shared personal experiences, often in a humorous and/or supportive manner; with relatively few videos presenting information or giving advice. The majority of videos discussed the creator’s own experiences with mental health, with few videos created by self-described mental health experts. Harmful elements, such as pro-suicide or eating disorder messages, were rare. We identified strong gendered patterns in both the creators and viewers of mental health videos, pointing to specific areas of concern for girls (eating disorders and body image) and boys (suicide). Overall, this content analysis paints a nuanced picture of the mental health content viewed by adolescents. Findings highlight the need for more expansive theories of the multifaceted impacts of mental health content, and for interventions that empower adolescents to capitalize on the opportunities provided by this content while minimizing potential harms.

articles.title: Over 3,000 voices: Understanding how climate change shapes the minds and lives of young people in Australia
articles.authors: Samantha Julia Legaspi Eala; Caroline X. Gao; Yan Zhang; Hasini Gunasiri; Rebecca Patrick; Kate Filia; Sunny N Nguyen; Neerja Singh; Shu Mei Teo; Emma Lawrance
articles.abstract:
Young people are especially vulnerable to the mental health impacts of climate change. Yet the mechanisms linking climate change to mental health remain unclear. This study explored how climate change shapes the emotions, thoughts, and behaviours of young people from Australia, and the implications for wellbeing.
Data were drawn from Mission Australia’s 2023 Youth Survey. Participants were asked to describe how climate change impacts their thinking, feelings, and behaviour. Free-text responses from 3,272 participants were analysed using inductive thematic analysis, with relational analysis identifying interconnected patterns across emotional, cognitive, and behavioural domains.
Young people from Australia reported diverse responses to climate change, including feelings of anxiety, sadness, and hope; thoughts about future impacts, personal responsibility, and systemic failure; and behaviours ranging from pro-environmental actions to disengagement. Based on overlapping feelings, thinking, and behaviour, seven archetypes of response were identified: the Hopeless Helper, Nervous Navigator, Furious Fighter, Guilty Guardian, Wounded Witness, Detached Drifter, and Determined Doer.
Findings highlight the complex and interconnected ways young people respond to climate change across emotions, thoughts, and behaviours. Archetypes provide a framework for understanding both risks and resilience, emphasising that distress often stems from systemic inaction. They underscore the need for nuanced measures, tailored interventions, and policies that systematically integrate climate and mental health.

articles.title: Adolescent Perspectives on Parental Consent Requirements for Depression Treatment: A Mixed-Methods Investigation
articles.authors: Amanda Smock; Tubanji Walubita; Andy Rapoport; Shannon Hill; Aileen Kangavary; Riley McDanal; Mallory Dobias; Juan Pablo Zapata; Briana Shiri Last; Jessica L. Schleider
articles.abstract: Objective: Depression incidence in adolescents is increasing, yet most do not access treatment. Policies requiring parental consent to initiate care may influence adolescent treatment access. We explored adolescent perspectives toward accessing treatment with and without parental consent (i.e., self-consent) across four modalities: therapy (in-person and online) and self-guided supports (in-person and online). We explored differences in attitudes amongst sub-samples, demographics, and depression severity. Method: 43 adolescents participated in an online survey and interviews (MAge= 15.5; 65.1% cisgender girl/woman; 41.9% non-Hispanic White); one sub-sample required parental consent (n = 29), and one self-consented (n = 14) (i.e., parental consent requirements waived). We used a multi-step analytic approach. Using content analysis, we qualitatively coded a positive, negative, or mixed valence to indicate attitudes toward parental consent or self-consent, and calculated frequencies. Using thematic analysis, themes were informed by self-determination theory. Results: Three themes were identified: Factors that Influence Adolescent (1) Autonomy, (2) Competence, and (3) Relatedness. Generally, adolescents viewed self-consent positively, seeing it as preserving their autonomy and decision-making. Self-consent attitudes were consistently positive for self-guided supports and more mixed for therapist-delivered treatments. The ‘waived parental consent’ sub-sample expressed more positive self-consent attitudes overall; younger adolescents described more negative attitudes and adolescents with less severe depression symptoms described more negative and mixed attitudes. Conclusions: Perspectives on parent consent requirements were not monolithic, and were shaped by developmental needs for self-determination. Results suggest supporting adolescents' competence to navigate treatments; preserving autonomy in decision-making; and strengthening parent-teen communication and relatedness to encourage help-seeking.

articles.title: Righteous Wrongs: Moral Judgments of Ideologically Motivated Transgressions
articles.authors: Éloïse Côté; Jennifer Ellen Stellar
articles.abstract: With growing political polarization, ideologically motivated transgressive and even violent behaviour appears to be on the rise. For those engaging in this behaviour, the transgression may seem justified if it serves a loftier ideological goal, but how do observers perceive these kinds of transgressions? Across five studies we investigated how observers evaluate ideologically motivated transgressions and considered the impact of observers’ ideological alignment with the transgressor. We measured perceptions of the motivation behind a recent assassination of a political advocate (Study 1) and used hypothetical scenarios to experimentally probe these effects and test mechanisms (Studies 2-5). Ideologically motivated transgressions were met with equivalently harsh judgments by observers compared to selfish or sadistically motivated transgressions. However, this effect was heavily moderated by an asymmetrical effect of ideological alignment. When observers shared the ideological views of the transgressor was their moral judgment more lenient, compared to selfish or sadistically motivated acts, while holding opposing ideological views generally elicited equivalent moral judgments. Justifying the transgression as a means to an end and viewing the transgressor as heroically sacrificing for the cause explained these effects. These findings have implications for how ideologically motivated transgressions are communicated and policed.

articles.title: AI-Assisted Language Sample Analysis Identifies Linguistic Markers of Children’s Social and Cognitive Development
articles.authors: Jessica Michael Lammert; Blake Edward Butler; Emiko Osborne; Sreethan Vuppala
articles.abstract: Narrative-based Language Sample Analysis (LSA) is an informative approach for evaluating school-aged children’s social and cognitive development. Traditionally, LSA has relied on human evaluations, which are often subjective and require significant time and resources. Recent advances in Natural Language Processing (NLP) have made automating LSA easier and more accurate than ever before, yet the effectiveness of this approach remains largely unexplored. The current study sought to determine whether NLP can be used to extract features from narrative retelling samples that are useful for predicting cognitive and social skills in school-aged children. We used data from the Healthy Brain Network, a large open access pediatric database (N = 242; aged 6 – 16), where children watched a short animated movie, answered objective comprehension questions, and retold what happened in the movie in their own words. We used Coh-Metrix, a computational tool for discourse analysis, to automatically extract several linguistic features of interest from the resulting narrative language samples. Several NLP-extracted features were predictive of social difficulties, phonemic decoding ability, age, socioeconomic status, and language screener scores (R2 = 0.12 – 0.37). Moreover, NLP-extracted features frequently improved predictions over objective question accuracy (∆R2 = 0.11 – 0.15). These findings demonstrate the ability of automated approaches to improve the efficiency of LSA and complement traditional assessment methods.

articles.title: Subskills Underlying Children’s Eye Movements During Passage Reading
articles.authors: Charlotte Jeppsen; Leah Zimmermann; Keith Baxelbaum; Bob McMurray
articles.abstract:
Purpose. Skilled readers use complex eye-movement patterns to understand passages. Eye-movement indices, (i.e., first fixation duration, regressions; Rayner, 1997) are thought to reflect cognitive processes (i.e., word reading or syntactic reanalysis). This work has primarily focused on linking these indices to text-level variation. Less work has linked indices to individual differences in subskills, (e.g., word recognition), which could illuminate real-time cognitive processing in developing readers.

Method. Eye-movement indices were analyzed from 212 English-speaking children (107 male, 105 female; Grade: M = 4.00, SD = 0.76) silently reading six passages. Age, decoding and oral language skills, real-time word recognition (Visual World Paradigm) and oculomotor coordination were related to these indices using commonality analyses. 
Results. Accurate and efficient word recognition accounted for unique variance across both word-level (fixation duration) and sentence level (regression) indices.  Age only uniquely predicted shorter word reading durations and inaccurate oculomotor control predicted longer regressions. Oral language skill explained very little unique variance across indices. 

Conclusion. Both accurate and efficient word recognition are critical to the development of passage reading, while oculomotor control and oral language effects are more limited. Together, these results suggest that word recognition skills are the major bottleneck for young readers.

articles.title: iOS Shortcuts as a Free, No-Code Tool for Event-Triggered Experience Sampling
articles.authors: Douglas A. Parry; Tilo Hartmann
articles.abstract: Event-triggered experience sampling prompts in situ surveys when specific behaviors or contexts occur. This approach is valuable for capturing infrequent or context-bound experiences but often requires custom or expensive software. This article describes how iOS Shortcuts, a pre-installed automation feature, can provide a free, no-code alternative for event-triggered surveys on iPhones. Using trigger-action programming, researchers can configure automations that launch survey URLs with embedded contextual parameters when designated events occur. We describe the procedure, outline a workflow of triggers, actions, and embedded variables, and illustrate the approach with worked examples and templates.

articles.title: Does collective identification with moral convictions explain intolerance? Not just “us” versus “them”
articles.authors: Pierce D. Ekstrom; Lindsay Novak
articles.abstract: Although people often tolerate disagreement in attitude domains that concern matters of personal taste or social convention, they are much less tolerant of disagreement about moral convictions—attitudes that they construe as matters of right and wrong. The current studies test a novel theory that this ostensibly unique intolerance for moral disagreement is simply a special case of identity-based prejudice. This theory holds that moral convictions are identity-central components of the collective self, and that intolerance for moral disagreement can be explained by a tendency to use moral convictions to distinguish a moral “us” from an immoral “them.” Consistent with this theory, we found that moral conviction was associated with both self-report and reaction-time measures of identity centrality with remarkable consistency, suggesting that relatively moralized attitudes are almost always at least relatively central to the self-concept. We also found (using a recall-based task of social categorization) that participants were more likely to use their moral convictions to categorize others to the extent that participants identified with those convictions. Inconsistent with our theory, however, we found that political and social intolerance for moral disagreement were unrelated to social categorization processes; moreover, participants’ collective identification with the group of people who shared their moral convictions accounted for little if any of the link between attitude-level moral conviction and intolerance for dissimilar others. We conclude that although moral convictions are very often central to identity and invoke collectives of like-minded others, moral disagreement is not just a matter of “us” versus “them.”

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence Systems Distort Upstream Selection in Human Social Learning
articles.authors: William J. Brady; Chen-Wei Yu; Nicholas Ornstein; Bolun Sun; Joshua Conrad Jackson
articles.abstract: Humans are social learners who depend on observing others to acquire knowledge, norms, and behaviors, a capacity that underlies cumulative cultural evolution. Social learning unfolds in two stages: upstream selection determines what information becomes visible, and downstream selection determines what learners copy from that visible sample. Downstream selection occurs through biases such as conformity bias (copying what appears common) and prestige bias (copying those who appear highly respected). These downstream biases can be adaptive when upstream selection yields a sample that reflects the population's true distribution, so that what appears common is actually common and those who appear respected are actually competent. We argue that digital technologies disrupt this condition, creating an upstream selection problem. Engagement-based algorithms amplify the tails of the distribution, surfacing rare and extreme content, whereas generative AI collapses it toward the mode (of the population or the user), erasing the surrounding diversity. Crucially, in each system the optimization signal shapes both visibility and prestige. For engagement-based algorithms, the signal is engagement: creators who post extreme content become more visible and, through the likes, shares, and followers, appear more prestigious. For generative AI, the signal is statistical typicality: it makes a modal answer dominant and, with no alternatives shown, makes the model that produced it appear more prestigious. These distortions can give rise to emergent group-level phenomena, including pluralistic ignorance and illusory consensus. Synthesizing evidence across psychology, cultural evolution, and computational social science, we provide a framework for how digital technologies disrupt social learning and outline interventions for restoring functional cultural transmission.

articles.title: All BANG, little buck: Need-related experiences are weakly linked with behavior in the video game domain
articles.authors: Nick Ballou; Tamás Andrei Földes; Matti Vuorre; Thomas Hakman; Kristoffer Magnusson; Andrew K Przybylski
articles.abstract: Psychological theories of media use often assume that subjective motivation affects observable behavior. Using video games as a test case, we examine this assumption by pairing repeated self-reports of motivation with objective digital trace data at scale. Across two datasets comprising tens of thousands of hours of gaming behavior, we test predictions derived from self-determination theory and the Basic Needs in Games (BANG) model, which posit that autonomy, competence, and relatedness experiences drive engagement. Study 1 (preregistered) analyzes 11k daily observations from 555 U.S. players with 30 days of multi-platform digital trace data. Study 2 (exploratory) examines 102k sessions from 9k PowerWash Simulator players, linking in-game experience prompts to behavioral logs. In both studies, need satisfaction was robustly associated with subjective states but showed weak or null associations with short-term gaming behavior, including subsequent play, session length, and return latency, across extensive preregistered and robustness analyses. These findings reveal a substantial motivation–behavior gap and suggest that SDT-based accounts may overestimate the role of need satisfaction in explaining when or how much people play. Data and code are available under a CC0 license at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18352505.

articles.title: Open Play: A longitudinal dataset of multi-platform video game digital trace data and psychological measures
articles.authors: Nick Ballou; Tamás Andrei Földes; Matti Vuorre; Thomas Hakman; Kristoffer Magnusson; Andrew K Przybylski
articles.abstract: A major limitation to understanding digital technology use, and its potential psychological consequences, is the lack of sufficiently detailed, multidimensional, and accurate data. We present a dataset of 2.0K individuals’ video game play telemetry data from Nintendo Switch, Steam, and Xbox, paired with psychological measures across multiple dimensions of mental health, motivations, well-being, and cognitive ability. The data were collected under a preregistered design that included 12 weeks of survey data (thirty daily surveys, six biweekly surveys, three biweekly cognitive tests), and digital trace data for 43 months. Cleaned data include 1.5M hours of video game play across 10,475 titles, 23K responses to 14 survey instruments, and 2.9K attention ability measures to facilitate examining longitudinal associations between play behaviors and psychological functioning. Data and codebook are available under a CC0 (with supplemental reidentification clause) license at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17536656.

articles.title: The social filtering of reason quality: Evidence from a partisan penalty
articles.authors: Breanna K. Nguyen; Mandy Fuller; Walter Sinnott-Armstrong; Samuel Murray
articles.abstract: When people evaluate another person's view, they sometimes evaluate not only the belief but the reasons offered in its support. These evaluations can come apart: two people can agree on a conclusion and still dismiss each other's reasons as weak or unserious. We tested whether judgments of reason quality are socially filtered, such that reasons associated with political opponents are evaluated less favorably than reasons associated with political allies. Across four preregistered studies (N = 4,049), we used contemporary partisanship in the United States as a test case. Participants rated the quality of political reasons supporting or opposing positions they had endorsed or rejected. Studies 1a and 2 established a partisan penalty: reasons associated with participants’ own party received higher ratings than reasons associated with the opposing party, even when the reasons supported positions participants shared. Study 1b showed that unlabeled reasons carried reliable partisan signals. Study 3 linked each participant’s source inferences to that participant’s evaluations of the same reasons. Reasons inferred to come from a contrapartisan received lower ratings, and this association remained after adjusting for perceived factual accuracy and shared values. These findings suggest that perceived partisan affiliation is associated with reason-quality judgments beyond differences in participants’ stated positions.

articles.title: The effect of the shapes of plotting symbols on their perceived positions
articles.authors: Tadamasa Sawada; Sarkis Kalikian; Habet Madoyan
articles.abstract: The scatter plot primarily uses the positions of symbols to represent variables. This study tested how the perception of the symbols’ positions could be affected by their shapes in a behavioral experiment. The results of the experiment showed that the accuracy and precision of the perceived position depends on the symbols’ shapes. The perceived positions of the circle, the square, and the diamond were accurate and precise while the perceived position of the triangle was not. Based on the results and the existing knowledge of the visual system, we discuss the critical properties of the symbols’ shapes for the perception of their positions, and we propose new symbols for the scatter plot.

articles.title: Identity-Based Transdiagnostic Therapy (IBTT) for young people with anxiety and depression: A study protocol for a multicenter randomized clinical trial
articles.authors: Guillem Feixas; Giuseppina Rametti; Irene Álvarez Tomás; Sergi Corbella; Danielle Mullins; Clara Paz; Sonia Lorente; Miquel Alabèrnia-Segura
articles.abstract: Background: Youth mental health is a pressing global concern, with depression and anxiety being prevalent disorders. The unique challenges of adolescents and youth are underrepresented in psychotherapy research, and existing transdiagnostic treatments target symptom mechanisms rather than identity processes. In response, we propose a novel treatment modality: Identity-Based Transdiagnostic Therapy (IBTT). This approach utilizes the repertory grid technique with Explore Your Meanings (EYME), a digital tool incorporating an automated interview to elicit the person’s construal about self and others, and a virtual reality (VR) scenario to explore their identity system. Methods: With a two-arm, parallel, assessor-blinded, multicenter, randomized clinical trial (RCT) with a three-month follow-up, we will examine the efficacy of IBTT compared to the Unified Protocol (a validated CBT treatment). To ensure enough statistical power, we target a sample of 128 participants aged 16-29 years to be randomly allocated (ratio 1:1) to receive a maximum of 16 sessions of either intervention. The primary outcome will be the between-group difference in symptom change from baseline to post-treatment and follow-up, as measured by the total score of the Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Scales (DASS-21). Discussion: Evidence supporting the efficacy of this innovative approach would likely have a substantial impact on clinical practice for young adults and enhance engagement throughout the psychotherapy process.

articles.title: Media portrayals of youth self-harm and suicide: An examination social determinants and inequalities
articles.authors: Leigh Huggard; Daisy Wiggin; Eve Griffin; Elaine McMahon
articles.abstract: Increasing evidence shows that social inequalities are central determinants of youth self harm and suicide. Media coverage shapes public understanding of these risk factors, yet little is known how Irish news outlets portray them. The study examined the representation of determinants in popular Irish print and online news between 2023 and 2025. Following a systematic keyword search of eight major outlets, 918 articles were examined, of which 25% contained at least one causal explanation. Using abductive content analysis guided by the WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health framework, articles were coded for type of causal explanation, source of the explanation, and social characteristics of described individuals. Frequency counts and chi square tests assessed differences by year, publication, source, gender of described individuals, and whether the explanation referred to suicide, self harm, or both. Psychosocial explanations dominated (71% of mentions), driven by abuse/trauma (37%) relational factors (23%), and technology and social media use (17%). Macro-level structural determinants such as wider political, socioeconomic, or cultural contexts were less frequently mentioned, and no biological factors were reported. Female experiences were over represented (62% of profiles), and explanations were most commonly supplied by lived-experience accounts (20%) and non-expert professionals, such as politicians or teachers (17%). No temporal trend was observed, and there were limited differences in explanations for self-harm vs suicide. The findings reveal a media landscape that foregrounds individual level narratives and under represents systemic risk factors. Extending Irish suicide reporting guidelines to require inclusion of structural determinants and expert perspectives could improve public awareness, reduce stigma, and bolster evidence based prevention strategies.

articles_hidden.title: Investigating the effect of briefing modality on participant experiences, data quality, and data quantity in an experience sampling study
articles_hidden.authors: Elisabeth Hutasoit; Milla Pihlajamäki; Ginette Lafit; Olivia J Kirtley; Inez Myin-Germeys; Gudrun Eisele
articles_hidden.abstract: The Experience Sampling Method (ESM) requires participants to repeatedly complete assessments in daily life, typically without direct researcher supervision. Participant briefing is therefore an important opportunity to prepare participants to follow the protocol independently, but the effects of different characteristics of briefings are poorly understood. This quasi-experimental study examined whether online versus in-person briefing influenced data quantity (compliance), data quality (careless responding), and participant experiences (participant burden, perceived briefing sufficiency). First-year psychology students (N=249) were assigned to an online (n=209) or in-person (n=40) briefing condition based on recruitment phase and completed a seven-day ESM protocol with 10 daily prompts. Results showed that briefing modality did not significantly affect mean levels of compliance, careless responding, participant burden, or perceived briefing sufficiency. However, the effect of briefing modality on compliance changed over time: initial compliance was higher and declined more steeply in the online briefing condition than in the in-person briefing condition, although both conditions reached descriptively similar compliance rates by the end of the study. No significant interactions with time were found for careless responding or momentary burden. These findings suggest that online briefing may be a viable alternative to in-person briefing in relatively short and straightforward ESM protocols. However, in-person briefing may support more sustained compliance over time. Future research should replicate these findings in fully experimental designs and examine whether briefing modality matters more in other samples or longer or more demanding ESM studies.

articles_hidden.title: Dietary Modulation of Neurobiological Mechanisms Underlying Executive Function and Decision-Making: A Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Iveta Harris; Ian Evans; Jessica Bayes; Mansi Das Singh
articles_hidden.abstract: Executive function (EF) and decision making (DM) are central to adaptive behaviour, yet evidence explaining how diet influences their underlying neurobiological mechanisms remains fragmented. This systematic review examined how dietary exposures influence the neurobiological mechanisms underlying EF and DM. The review followed PRISMA guidelines and was prospectively registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251173091). Of 12,952 records identified, 26 studies met the inclusion criteria, involving over 2,000 participants. Across the included studies, dietary exposures were associated with changes in metabolic, neurochemical, inflammatory, neural, and gut–brain pathways relevant to EF and DM. Behavioural effects were reported across all dietary domains but were less consistent than biological changes and varied according to intervention duration, task sensitivity, and participant characteristics. EF outcomes were more consistently modulated than DM outcomes, with effects most evident in working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility. Although less frequently studied, DM findings showed that dietary exposures could shift complex choices—including risk-taking, temporal discounting, and social decision-making—alongside changes in metabolic state and neurotransmitter precursor availability. Notably, none of the reviewed studies specifically examined ultra-processed food exposure, identifying an important gap in the current evidence. Few studies examined when or how biological changes translated into measurable behavioural outcomes. Together, the findings suggest that dietary effects may emerge across biological systems before consistent changes in EF and DM become detectable, potentially explaining variability in previous behavioural findings. Longitudinal, mechanistically integrated studies that account for potential confounding factors, including hormonal status, background dietary intake, and participant characteristics, are needed to test this temporal sequence and determine when biological modulation produces cognitive and behavioural change.

articles_hidden.title: Is the Useful Field all you need on the road? Hazard localization performance in a gaze contingent scotoma paradigm
articles_hidden.authors: Ido Zivli; Jiali Song; Benjamin Wolfe
