We conclude limited evidence that children’s superior offline consolidation can compensate for weaknesses in memory integration.

articles_hidden.title: Reconceptualizing Individuals, Categories, and the Social Group: Self-Categorization Theory 2.0
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel Skorich
articles_hidden.abstract: Self-Categorization Theory is a theory of the way in which human beings come to represent themselves cognitively as group members. In this paper, I present 5 critiques of Self-Categorization Theory, with the goal of further refining it: (1) categorization into equivalence classes is neither sufficient nor necessary for perceiving groups as entities; (2) the boundary conditions on self-categorization (vs. categorization) are underspecified; (3) the person level is relatively underexamined; (4) meta-contrast is implausible as a basis for entity formation; and (5) comparative and correlational relations are overemphasized. I propose as resolutions to these critiques that: self-categorization is the categorization of intentional agents; groups are holistic entities, perceptually triggered by cues to collective intentionality, and cognitively represented as “conceptual atoms” with an associated object file; group phenomena have person equivalents and vice-versa; and relations between intentional entities and between intentional entities and their properties are represented propositionally in a “language of thought”. Taken together these resolutions result in an updated Self-Categorization Theory 2.0 (SCT2.0). I discuss this expanded theory in general terms, and then further elaborate on the key mechanisms of salience, depersonalization, and prototypicality. I conclude by emphasizing the way in which SCT2.0 builds on the legacy of its predecessor.

articles_hidden.title: FEED your mind: The evolutionary roots of human food cognition
articles_hidden.authors: Camille Rioux; Raffaella I Rumiati; Annie E. Wertz; Carol Coricelli
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on food cognition has largely overlooked that our modern food environment strongly differs from the environment in which our ancestors lived. When foraging for food in wild environments, our ancestors had to distinguish edible food resources from myriad inedible and potentially toxic entities. In contrast, in most cultures today, many decisions about food are made during a trip to the grocery store or a meal at a restaurant, where we might ask ourselves: Is this item healthy? but certainly not: Is this item edible or poisonous? Here we argue that the scope of the problem humans faced with respect to food included navigating through wild environments to Find candidate food items, Excluding the costs of making a mistake and consuming a harmful food item, Evaluating the nutritional benefits of the potential foods and Deciding which food items to include in their diet. We call this the FEED problem and argue that it provides an organizing framework for thinking about the wide array of cognitive processes involved in human food psychology. The FEED problem can also be used as a generative theory to produce new testable empirical predictions about what cognitive mechanisms drive our modern food behaviors and provides a roadmap for future research in the field of food cognition.

articles_hidden.title: Questionable mediated effect of peer victimization on prosocial behavior in adolescents: A reanalysis of Guo et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles_hidden.abstract: Using the covariance matrix reported by Guo et al., we reassessed the evidence supporting their mediation model relating peer victimization to lower levels of prosocial behavior among adolescents. We demonstrate that the empirical associations can be reproduced with high accuracy by an alternative latent-variable model that does not depend on the order of influence proposed in the original article. In this model, self-reported peer victimization, psychological capital, empathy, and prosocial behavior are conceptualized as indicators of a broader latent construct, namely core self-evaluation. The findings illustrate a fundamental issue in observational research: different theoretical models may account equally well for the same covariance structure. Consequently, correlational data alone provide limited grounds for favoring one specific explanatory mechanism over competing alternatives. Consequently, researchers should consider alternative specifications before drawing strong conclusions about underlying processes.

articles_hidden.title: What Predicts Psychotherapy Outcomes Across Disorders and Treatments: an Umbrella Review
articles_hidden.authors: Niklas Jacobs; Tabea Jaleta; Kevin Hilbert
articles_hidden.abstract:
The objective of assigning patients to their most promising treatment has sparked considerable interest in 
contemporary research. Many studies develop models to predict treatment outcomes and stratify treatment 
allocation. Predictive accuracy of such models, however, has remained limited due to a lack of systematic 
information used for model training, given that variables included in such datasets are often selected due to their 
availability in routine care datasets. To increase systematic information in the data, the inclusion of promising 
candidate predictors, based on theoretical or empirical considerations, is crucial. Therefore, this study 
systematically searches for and summarizes the evidence on patient level variables that predict psychotherapy 
outcome. Since the literature to answer this question is vast, an umbrella review methodology (i.e., a review of 
reviews) was implemented. Searches in PubMed, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library with preregistered 
search strings yielded 5926 articles. Title and abstract screening implemented AI-based methods alongside 
human review. N = 51 papers were extracted and quantitative evidence was descriptively aggregated. We 
identified 69 potential predictors. Using post-hoc defined criteria, reliable and relevant predictors were selected. 
Some of these were known and frequently assessed predictors (e.g., symptom severity, diagnosis) while others 
are not frequently assessed in routine care. Among the latter were social support, executive functioning, 
therapeutic alliance and motivation for treatment. The identified variables represent promising candidate 
predictors, which can inform theoretical models of therapy success, guide clinicians, or, if included in future 
analysis pipelines, have the potential to increase predictive performance in psychotherapy studies.

articles_hidden.title: Social Coercion in the Shadow of Hierarchy: State-Mediated Coercive Mobilisation and Australians' COVID-19 Vaccination Compliance
articles_hidden.authors: Katie Attwell; Joshua Lake
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: This study investigates coercive (social) mobilisation to vaccinate in liberal democracies using evidence from Australia.
Methods: We analyse how government policies can prompt non-state actors to pressure the unvaccinated. We then analyse data on COVID-19 vaccination in a representative sample of adults (N=4208), investigating the prevalence and sources of coercive mobilisation and conducting regression analyses to identify associated factors.
Results: Conceptual analysis distinguished between state-led coercive mobilisation, where authoritarian governments rely on hierarchical structures to pressure citizens, and state-mediated coercive mobilisation, whereby liberal democratic governments generate social pressure through vaccine mandates that produce encourage stigmatisation, workplace expansion, and pressures associated with collective goals. Empirically, a quarter of people vaccinated reported being coerced, and more than half reported responding to some degree of social pressure. Social coercion was most common in New South Wales and Victoria. People were more likely to attribute vaccination to social coercion when they had lower political trust, or lower trust in friends and family as sources of vaccination information. Higher trust in social media sources and stronger community connectedness were associated with increased attribution to coercion. Higher education and socioeconomic status were associated with increased attributions of employer coercion, and education workers reported more social coercion. Younger people were consistently more likely to attribute vaccination to coercive mobilisation, with some evidence this was also true for women.

articles_hidden.title: What motivates support for mandatory vaccination? Trust as a moderator of relations between personal values and support for coercive policy measures

Self enhancement values (achievement; power) and tradition values generally showed the opposite pattern of effects, while conformity values displayed a relatively stronger (positive) direct effect. articles_hidden.title: ‘It is my life don’t take that choice from me’: Autistic young adults’ experiences, preferences and needs regarding autistic peer support
articles_hidden.authors: Tohid Zarei; Caelan Farr; Maxx Fischer; Summer Marchiori; KJ Hepworth; Caroline Ellison; Tobias Loetscher
articles_hidden.abstract: Autistic peer support, as a two-way system of help, is uniquely positioned to address high rates of loneliness and mental health challenges among autistic young adults. While following participatory research processes, we used reflexive thematic analysis to identify an overarching theme: flying together through shared understanding and shared struggles. This maps onto participants’ desire for reciprocal connections that enable understanding and safe unmasking, and their preference for in-person programs adapted to a range of support needs with meaningful participation in decision-making. Autistic Burnout and social connection were most participants’ preferred areas to be addressed. Especially when co-produced or peer-led, autistic peer support programs can contribute to providing a sense of collective movement with preserved self-determination for participants.

articles_hidden.title: Rescripting suicidal mental imagery in young people: A pilot study of feasibility, acceptability and safety
articles_hidden.authors: Lianne Schmaal; Georgie Paulik; Zamantha Munoz; Laura van Velzen; Pemma Davies; Martin Mitrevski; Eleanor Bailey; Phoebe Gleeson; Lisa Incerti; Samantha Galea
articles_hidden.abstract: Suicidal mental imagery – vivid, intrusive mental images of suicide or death - is common among young people experiencing suicidal ideation and may increase risk of suicidal behaviour, yet interventions directly targeting these images are lacking. articles_hidden.title: Neural correlates and behavioral outcomes of aesthetic chills and their prosthetic augmentation
articles_hidden.authors: Felix Schoeller; Leonardo Christov-Moore; Ninette Simonian; NA; Yaya Shi; Abhinandan Jain; Adam Horowitz; Velu Prabhakar Kumaravel; Ben Zhang; Micah Johnson

Chills carried a spatially distributed signature of attenuated theta power, elevated gamma power, and convergent increases across four independent complexity measures. Chills predicted self-transcendent phenomenology in a graded fashion across binary, frequency, and intensity operationalizations, yet predicted neither prosocial behavior nor schema change; both were instead predicted by the chills-locked neural signature, with distinct complexity measures tracking distinct outcome families. Thermal augmentation left the behavioral incidence of chills unchanged; in exploratory mediation models, however, it shifted chills-specific dynamics toward criticality and away from undifferentiated entropy, linking embodied augmentation to phenomenological, affective, prosocial, and schema outcomes. Aesthetic chills may therefore constitute an at least partially neuro-mimetic analogue of the psychedelic state, sharing its elevated signal diversity and a theta attenuation concordant with recent psilocybin electrophysiology, while gamma correspondence and the absence of psychedelic-typical alpha suppression remain unresolved.

articles_hidden.title: From Psychological States to Survey Responses: A Theory of Latent States and Response Style
articles_hidden.authors: Jess Grimmond; Scott Brown; Quentin Frederik Gronau; Guy Hawkins
articles_hidden.abstract:
Understanding human behaviour, thoughts, and experiences often relies on self-report measures,
yet responses frequently conflate multiple sources of information. We propose a theory in which
self-reported responses reflect both the constructs being assessed (latent states) and how
respondents choose to communicate that information (response style). We apply this theory to
Likert scale data through the Latent State and Response Style (LASARS) model, an
ordinal-probit approach that separates these sources of variance, yielding cleaner latent state
estimates and interpretable measures of response behaviour. LASARS represents response styles
as stable, three-dimensional signatures describing how individuals map internal experiences onto
response options. Our theory enables quantitative tests of previously difficult-to-evaluate
predictions. Across a series of empirical studies, we show that response styles can be selectively
adjusted to task demands without corresponding changes in latent state expression, and that they
are relatively stable across time and survey instruments, often matching or exceeding the stability
of latent psychological states. We also support a novel prediction: response style information
from one survey can be used to deconfound response style from substantive latent state signal in a
separate survey, even when that survey cannot identify the two. Together, these findings support a
unified theory of self-report responding in which response styles are meaningful, stable, and
informative individual differences rather than mere measurement error. LASARS, therefore,
provides a principled framework for improving the precision, interpretability, and validity of
survey-based measurement.

articles_hidden.title: Unsupervised Careless Responding Detection: A Comprehensive Comparison between Model-based and Model-Agnostic Approaches
articles_hidden.authors: Wenshuo Li; Carl F. Falk
articles_hidden.abstract: Careless responding (CR) is a major concern for data quality in the social sciences. It is common for researchers to attempt to detect and filter out CR at the respondent level. Though various choices are available, detection methods relying solely on response data have received much attention since they do not require the collection of additional information. Along these lines, model-based approaches to CR detection rely on specifying distinct measurement models for careful and careless respondents in a mixture model. In contrast, model-agnostic methods aim to identify thresholds of careless respondent indices, making classifications without reliance on measurement models. Although these two streams share some common assumptions for CR, these methods have been developed in parallel and have not been directly compared. To systematically compare these two streams of approaches, we conducted three large-scale simulation studies manipulating the number of items, proportion of reverse-coded items, contamination rates, carelessness types, presence of model misspecification, item properties, as well as sample sizes. To balance generalizability and realism, conditions for the first two simulations were inspired by real instruments from personality and health outcome measures, while the third simulation study explicitly manipulated item properties to de-confound naturally occurring variability induced under the first two studies. Generally, results indicate that model-based approaches are more specificity-focused and should be preferred under lower contamination rates and fewer items, while model-agnostic approaches are sensitivity-focused and outperform model-based approaches under other contamination rates and more CR types provided there are a sufficient number of items.

articles_hidden.title: Using reinforcement learning to explain psychodynamics
articles_hidden.authors: Zack Dulberg; Jonathan D. Cohen
articles_hidden.abstract: In this article we consider the use of reinforcement learning (RL) as a formal framework for understanding traditional psychodynamic phenomena. We show how RL can be used to provide new insights as well as normative explanations for key psychodynamic constructs, grounding them in principles of reward maximization and adaptation. We conclude that, by providing a computational foundation for psychodynamic concepts, RL may contribute to the development of a more rigorous science of psychological dynamics and their disruption in clinical conditions.

articles_hidden.title: Sincronicidad Facial y Contacto Visual en Telemedicina  mediante Visión por Computadora
articles_hidden.authors: Rodrigo Miguel Bermúdez Alemón; Daniela Carolina Rosero Córdoba; ivan arango; Lidia Márquez Márquez; Santiago Castiello
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introducción y Objetivo: La transición hacia la telepsiquiatría—una instancia de la telemedicina—ha generado interrogantes sobre cómo la mediación digital afecta la Comunicación No Verbal (CNV) y la consolidación de la relación médico-paciente. Este estudio tuvo como objetivo principal evaluar el impacto de la sincronía facial y el contacto visual mediado por computadora sobre la alianza terapéutica y la percepción de la calidad asistencial en pacientes adultos con trastornos de la personalidad.
Métodos: Se llevó a cabo un estudio observacional, descriptivo y transversal. La muestra consistió en 25 videograbaciones de teleconsultas psiquiátricas subsecuentes (N=25; n[fotogramas]>1,000,000) realizadas a través de la plataforma Zoom en el Instituto Nacional de Psiquiatría Ramón de la Fuente Muñiz (INPRFM). La alianza terapéutica se evaluó cuantitativamente empleando el Working Alliance Inventory en sus versiones para paciente (WAI-P) y clínico (WAI-T). Para el procesamiento biométrico, se utilizaron scripts personalizados y un software de visión por computadora. Este modelo extrajo series temporales de activación de Unidades de Acción (AU) faciales y vectores algorítmicos en grados de la dirección de la mirada, permitiendo modelar la Sincronía Facial Global y el contacto visual recíproco.
Resultados: No se encontraron correlaciones estadísticamente significativas entre la Sincronía Facial Global o el contacto visual y la alianza terapéutica (WAI-P y WAI-T). De forma homóloga, se observó una ausencia de correlación entre los reportes de alianza relacional del clínico y del paciente. Sin embargo, un análisis intrasesión detectó un aumento en la Sincronía Facial General al final de la teleconsulta. 
Conclusiones: Este estudio es la prueba de concepto para el uso de visión por computadora para analizar CNV en telemedicina. Investigaciones futuras deben considerar la dinámica temporal de la interacción durante la telemedicina. Aquí describimos el método para que unidades de telemdicina puedan llevar a cabo análisis de CNV mediante visión por computadora.

articles_hidden.title: Initial Development of the Hypomanic Tendency Scales (HTS): A Multidimensional Measure of Personality Dimensions Associated with Hypomania
articles_hidden.authors: Kasey Stanton; Jack D Burke; Helena Towne; Isabella Whitesides; Holly Frances Levin-Aspenson; Noah N. Emery; Corinne Carlton
articles_hidden.abstract: A range of tools have been developed for assessing hypomania/mania risk and/or personality and temperament styles related to hypomania. articles_hidden.title: Genetic syndromes
articles_hidden.authors: Caroline G. Richter; Kaylie Burns; Phuong Ta; Wanqin Yu
articles_hidden.abstract:
•	Genetic syndromes are dynamic developmental conditions rather than fixed gene-to-behavior outcomes; genetic alterations set initial constraints that interact with health, learning, family, and educational contexts to shape probabilistic developmental trajectories.
•	Turner, Klinefelter, and Marfan syndromes show that a genetic diagnosis does not imply intellectual disability: selective cognitive, academic, or medical vulnerabilities can occur alongside broadly preserved general intellectual functioning.
•	Down syndrome and Williams syndrome are compared across etiology, medical comorbidities, motor skills, language, literacy, mathematics, executive functioning, sleep, social behavior, and adaptive functioning, revealing contrasting profiles.
•	Information-processing, neuroconstructivist, and dynamic-systems accounts, including cumulative risk-and-resilience and family-systems models, explain how syndrome-related profiles emerge through developmental cascades rather than being directly specified by genetic etiology.
•	Assessment and intervention should extend beyond IQ to component processes, longitudinal change, self-report from the individual, probabilistic prognosis, and modifiable environments and instruction, such as systematic phonics for reading.

articles_hidden.title: Achievement motives and anxiety are associated with persistence for delayed rewards
articles_hidden.authors: Avital Miller; Karolina Maria Lempert
articles_hidden.abstract: People vary in how long they are willing to persist for delayed rewards when the timing of those rewards is uncertain. Decisions about when to give up on delayed rewards result from a dynamic decision-making process in which people weigh the benefits of continued waiting against the opportunity costs of waiting. We hypothesized that individual differences in persistence might therefore emerge from differences in motivation, with approach motives (i.e., hope for success) predicting increased persistence and avoidance motives (i.e., fear of failure) predicting reduced persistence. In an online study, participants (n = 284) completed self-report questionnaires and a decision-making task optimized to capture individual differences in persistence. Hope for Success and Fear of Failure were assessed with the Achievement Motives Scale. Hope for Success was significantly positively associated with persistence, a relationship that was robust to controlling for relevant demographic covariates. Fear of Failure was negatively associated with persistence, but this association was only marginally significant after controlling for covariates. Reduced persistence predicted alcohol use intensity, replicating previous research. Finally, exploratory analyses demonstrated a significant association between anxious-depression and reduced persistence. Together, these findings suggest that persistence is linked to individual differences in motivational orientation and related psychological characteristics.

articles_hidden.title: Reduced theta-gamma coupling during real-world episodic encoding
articles_hidden.authors: Alireza Taheritorbati; Jane O'Connor; Tel Silito; Keva Klamer; Shaylyn Kress; Niayesh Allahdad; Jordyn Alicia Musial; Jared Rollingson; joshua Craig; Mary-Lou Gregoire
articles_hidden.abstract: Episodic memories are rarely formed under the controlled, simplified conditions typical of laboratory research. They are built from continuous, embodied experiences unfolding in real time and real space. Coupling between frontal theta and parietal gamma activity was computed during encoding as an index of this cross-frequency coordination, and free-recall memory was assessed immediately after. Real-world encoding was associated with significantly lower frontal theta to parietal gamma PAC than 2D encoding, even though recall performance did not differ between conditions. PAC positively predicted recall only in the 2D condition, with no equivalent relationship emerging for Real-world encoding. In the Real-world condition, PAC was negatively correlated with general cognitive ability, suggesting that higher cognitive functioning requires less cross-frequency coordination during naturalistic encoding. Together, these findings position theta-gamma PAC as a compensatory neural mechanism, recruited more heavily when the encoding environment provides less external structure. This suggests that real-world experiences may place a lighter coordination burden on the encoding brain, consistent with a compensatory account of theta-gamma PAC.

articles_hidden.title: Not All Spiritual Bypass Is the Same: Divergent Network Roles Across Spirituality, Forgiveness, and Psychological Resources
articles_hidden.authors: Sebastian Binyamin Skalski-Bednarz; Jacek Prusak; Paweł Dudzik; Edyta Charzyńska; Jon R. Webb
articles_hidden.abstract: Spiritual bypass, the use of spiritual beliefs and practices to sidestep unresolved psychological difficulty, comprises two dimensions, psychological avoidance and spiritualizing, which may relate differently to psychospiritual constructs. This chapter used a network approach to examine how these two dimensions, alongside three dimensions of spirituality (ritualistic, theistic, existential), three dimensions of dispositional forgiveness (self, others, uncontrollable situations) plus feeling forgiven by God, and three additional positive resources (hope, gratitude, self-compassion), are organized as a set of direct, facet-level associations rather than as broader, undifferentiated domains. articles_hidden.title: Measurement factors influencing caregiver involvement in child health studies: A mixed-methods study
articles_hidden.authors: Moira Duffy; Laoise Kelly; Eibhlín Looney; Dimity Dutch; Brittany J Johnson; Lucy Porter; Sarah Redsell; Karen Matvienko-Sikar
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. How outcomes are measured in studies can influence recruitment, retention, and data quality. This study examined characteristics of outcome measurement instruments influencing caregivers’ data provision in child health studies. 

Methods. An online mixed-methods cross-sectional survey including 22 closed-ended and one open-ended question(s) about outcome measurement instrument related factors influencing data provision in child health studies. Quantitative data were descriptively analyzed; qualitative data were analyzed using content analysis. 

Results. The survey was conducted with 490 caregivers of a child ≤12 years. The most important characteristics influencing caregivers’ provision of data were potential risk or discomfort to their child, ease of data provision, and perception of potential benefit to others. Caregivers ranked online data provision as their highest preference (M 1.23, SD 0.53; lower score indicates higher preference). Caregivers’ highest preferences were for healthcare professional data collection (M 2.50, SD 1.29), providing data in their own time (M 1.68, SD 1.27), and in their own homes (M 1.38, SD 0.88). Qualitative data indicated that trust, time and ease, perceived research value, and child comfort and safety were important to caregivers.   

Conclusions. Enhancing child comfort/safety, caregiver understanding/trust, and ease of data collection in child health studies is vital to maximize data provision and quality. Doing so, can improve evaluation of treatments and interventions, and improve child health outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: The Social Prioritisation Gradient: Gender, Age and Personality Shape the Relative Salience of Self, Friends, and Strangers
articles_hidden.authors: Meike Scheller; Naomi Lee; Jie Sui
articles_hidden.abstract: Why do people differ in how they prioritise social information? Enhanced processing of self-relevant information is among the most reliable effects in social cognition, but individuals vary considerably in how strongly different social identities are prioritised. The present study asked where along the self–friend–stranger gradient individual differences emerge. We combined data from eight experiments using the shape-label matching task with Big Five personality questionnaire measures. At the group-level, participants showed a robust gradient of social prioritisation, with self-associated information processed most efficiently, followed by friend- and stranger-associated information. Despite this consistency, substantial inter-individual variation was evident, reflected in the malleability of processing of others rather of the self: Gender, Openness, and Extraversion emerged as the most robust predictors of social identity processing performance: gender and Extraversion were particularly associated with friend-related processing, and Openness with the separation of strangers from socially closer identities. Age moderated several personality-related effects across the social gradient, though less consistently and in a young-skewed sample. Together, the findings suggest that individual differences in social prioritisation appear to arise less from how strongly the self is prioritised than from how socially close and distant others are weighted around it.

articles_hidden.title: The Brain Dynamical Repertoire and the Evolution of Clinical Symptoms
articles_hidden.authors: Damien Depannemaecker; Florencia Altschuler; Hélène Soydemir; Gabriele Casagrande; Cecilia Gonzalez Campo; Pierpaolo Sorrentino; Antoine Lefrère; Christophe Gauld; VIktor Jirsa
articles_hidden.abstract: The brain continuously reconfigures through a repertoire of transient states and transitions. However, most studies on neuropsychiatric disorders still relate symptoms to static or time-averaged measures of brain organization. Here, we review emerging evidence that clinically relevant information is also contained in the brain dynamical repertoire, including the states accessible to an individual, their occupancy, persistence, and transition structure. Across psychiatric, neurodevelopmental, neurological, and neurodegenerative disorders, alterations in these dynamical features have been associated with symptom severity, cognitive impairment, functional outcome, and treatment response. Importantly, emerging longitudinal studies further suggest that brain dynamics can change with clinical state and, in some cases, provide information about subsequent symptom trajectories. We argue that these findings motivate a shift from viewing brain dynamics primarily as cross-sectional correlates of diagnostic categories toward examining how changes in an individual's dynamical repertoire relate to the evolution of symptoms over time.

articles_hidden.title: The Benefits of and Motivations Behind Large-Team Coordination in Psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Sajedeh Rasti; Krist Vaesen; Daniel Lakens
articles_hidden.abstract: To increase coordination in science in areas where this would be beneficial for knowledge generation, collaborative work needs to offer clear benefits to individual researchers. This study investigates the motivations for initiating large-team papers and the potential benefits of these projects in psychology. By qualitatively analyzing 500 papers, we find that large-team collaborations are most often instigated to deal with the practical challenges  inherent to complex research questions, but can also be motivated by broader social and or strategic factors. The results from quantitatively analyzing 1,699,513 papers published between 1975 and 2024 indicate that large-team collaborations are more likely to be cited and to appear in higher-ranked journals. Furthermore, their immediate impact on the field, as measured by citation counts within the first 2 years after publication, is on average higher than individually-authored papers. This suggests that contributing to collaborative projects in psychology will likely increase the number of high-rank journal publications to the resume of researchers. Overall, our findings indicate that large-team collaborations can be rewarding for individual researchers both by enabling early scientific impact and by contributing to stronger publication records.

articles_hidden.title: Mood stability and change map onto distinct insula-centered networks
articles_hidden.authors: Noa Danan; Michal Ramot; Hanna Keren
articles_hidden.abstract: Mood is changing continuously even when external events are minimal. These spontaneous mood dynamics may reveal how the brain maintains and modifies affective states. Yet mood is typically studied in response to external input, leaving the neural basis of spontaneous mood changes largely unknown. articles_hidden.title: The more, the better? Behavioral and neural correlates of frequent and infrequent vowel exposure

articles_hidden.title: The mental health of trans and gender-diverse populations: an umbrella review of systematic reviews with or without meta-analysis

articles_hidden.abstract:

articles_hidden.title: Remaking “The Unconscious” Paradigm, Act I: …The Gap” Between Subliminal Processing and the Unconscious “Mind…

articles_hidden.title: Potential Agency in the Absence of Actual Motor Control? Ownership-dependent Judgments in the Rubber Hand Illusion

articles_hidden.title: Estudio diacrónico de los snowclones del español: un análisis de corpus
articles_hidden.authors: Monika Lisowska; Bárbara Marqueta-Gracia; Antonio Benítez-Burraco
articles_hidden.abstract: En el presente artículo se aborda la productividad y evolución temporal de una selección de 60 estructuras semiidiomáticas conocidas como snowclones en español a partir de un corpus de textos correspondiente al periodo de 2011-2023. articles_hidden.title: Dense-Sampling the Menstrual Cycle Using EEG in a Single Case Study: Relating Markers of Cognitive Control and Mental Health

articles_hidden.title: From social input to social attention: Parental mood predictability is related to the development of gaze cueing
articles_hidden.authors: Dimana V. Atanassova; Marlene Meyer; Sabine Hunnius
articles_hidden.abstract:
Gaze following is a fundamental developmental milestone for social cognition. Adults’ attention is reliably cued by gaze shifts but less is known about how gaze cuing emerges in early childhood or what shapes its developmental trajectory. Reduced sensitivity to social input—such as gazes—and differences in the early social environment can affect the development of gaze cueing but the role of these factors remains untested.

By 3 years, an early form of the GCE was detectable, with children making more errors on gaze-incongruent trials. By 6 years, the effect was robustly established, yet remained sensitive to characteristics of children’s early social environment.

Contrary to our expectations, reduced social sensitivity indexed by higher callous-unemotional traits did not attenuate the GCE at any age; instead, at 3 years, it was associated with faster overall target detection. Parental mood unpredictability, indexing exposure to an inconsistent social environment, was associated with attenuated gaze cueing at 6 years. In contrast, greater parental mood negativity was associated with slower disengagement from gaze-incongruent targets.

Together, these findings map the developmental trajectory of gaze cueing across early childhood and highlight the role of the parental characteristics as a key factor in shaping early social-cognitive development.

articles_hidden.title: Revisiting Parental Strictness: Integrating When into How Parents Engage in Socialization
articles_hidden.authors: Huiguang Ren
articles_hidden.abstract: Parenting research has richly examined how parents socialize children, including whether responses are warm, controlling, autonomy-supportive, harsh, or culturally meaningful. This article argues that a complementary question remains undertheorized: when do parents respond and engage in socialization? I define parental strictness as the response thresholds through which parents decide whether children’s behavior is good or bad enough to warrant specific types of socialization. I next propose the Strictness Framework that distinguishes positive strictness from negative strictness, behavioral strictness from cognitive strictness, and their domain-specific patterns of stability and change. Crossing positive and negative strictness yields four strictness styles—disciplinarian, withholding, regulatory, and nurturing—that may shape children’s tendencies of engagement and disengagement as well as their openness to socialization. Integrating when into how parents engage in socialization clarifies familiar parenting patterns and generates new questions about development across cultures, contexts, and developmental domains.

articles_hidden.title: Why don't the victims of bullying seek help? The effect of underestimating bystanders’ defending intentions
articles_hidden.authors: Guanghui Chen; Zhang anyi; fan Wang; Li Chao; Pei Yongshun; Wei Cui; Wenxin Zhang
articles_hidden.abstract: Seeking help from others is an important strategy for coping with difficult situations; however, victims of bullying are often reluctant to seek help. Positive contextual information cues significantly reduced the underestimation bias and increased willingness to seek help, whereas negative contextual information cues significantly increased the underestimation bias and decreased willingness to seek help. These findings provide a plausible explanation for victims’ reluctance to seek help and offer practical implications for enhancing help-seeking willingness in school bullying prevention and intervention.

articles_hidden.title: The influence of audience presence in expert classical piano performance: Reliable reproduction with greater expressive variability
articles_hidden.authors: Emily A. Wood; Rory Kirk; Cameron J Anderson; Martin Alejandro Miguel; Laurel Trainor
articles_hidden.abstract: How the presence of an audience shapes skilled performance has been studied for over a century, largely through laboratory tasks testing whether being watched improves or impairs. We compared an expert pianist’s performance of the same six-piece programme alone in a private rehearsal and a public concert, measuring her motion, beat-level timing, sound intensity, and pedalling. The two performances were remarkably similar, with the pianist reproducing her expressive interpretation with high fidelity across every feature. Further, the passages she had marked as most expressive in the score were no more affected by the audience than the rest. Despite this overall consistency, audience presence introduced small but reliable changes: greater variability in her motion, timing, and soft pedal use, and at the least intense moments in the music (as rated by listeners) she drew out the tempo and shaped the quietest passages more with the soft pedal in concert. For this performer, an audience did not impair her performance but facilitated it, supporting a faithful execution of her prepared interpretation while increasing expression through enhanced variability.

articles_hidden.title: Randomized Trial of AI-Powered Mental Health Support  Embedded in University Academic Infrastructure
articles_hidden.authors: Julie Youko Anne Cachia; Xuan Zhao; Wenxi Pu; Chi Liao; merel Keijsers; Julian De Freitas; Peter Cornish; Rebecca Fortgang
articles_hidden.abstract: Realizing digital mental health’s promise in low-resourced settings requires a tool that works in real-world systems and that people engage with. articles_hidden.title: Eliciting Beliefs with Random Generation Tasks
articles_hidden.authors: Pablo Leon-Villagra; Lucas Castillo; Johanna Falben; Nick Chater; Adam N Sanborn
articles_hidden.abstract:
Elicitation methods, such as asking people to produce the deciles of a distribution, are standard practices in policy or applied statistics. Similarly, much of cognitive science and psychology focuses on determining people's people's beliefs or latent traits through questionnaires or judgment tasks. However, these approaches often only capture a rough outline of what people know and are usually limited to point estimates of people's beliefs. Here, we present a novel experimental paradigm that allows us to access people's beliefs and how variable these beliefs are. Our task is based on an established random generation paradigm in which participants produce quantities from a particular domain as randomly as possible. We hypothesize that due to the minds' general-purpose mechanisms for probabilistic inferences, these random sequences represent the participants' underlying prior beliefs. We show that our method can infer participants' beliefs for a wide range of numeric quantities at comparable accuracy as an established elicitation method.
Moreover, these inferred beliefs are consistent with individual participants' generalization and inference patterns in a subsequent conditional prediction task. We then extend our approach to non-numeric belief elicitation, highlighting how our method can go beyond numeric elicitation and provide insight into complex beliefs that are challenging to assess experimentally. Empirically, our results highlight that people know the rough shapes of environmental distributions, and these beliefs guide inference and generalization. Moreover, using our novel approach, we also show that people know the fine details of environmental distributions. Finally, our experimental results show that random generation paradigms can be a useful tool for cognitive scientists, psychologists, and applied statisticians.

articles_hidden.title: OpenDvM: Decoding the Visual Mind — A Unified Toolbox for EEG Attention Research
articles_hidden.authors: Dirk van Moorselaar; Sebastiaan Mathot; Stefan van der Stigchel
articles_hidden.abstract: Multivariate pattern analysis has become a standard complement to univariate event-related potentials (ERPs) in EEG research, yet integrated toolboxes that combine ERP, time-frequency, decoding, and forward-encoding analyses within a single, consistent framework remain largely confined to MATLAB. Developed with the needs of attention researchers specifically in mind, but readily applicable to other domains, OpenDvM computes stimulus- and response-locked ERPs and time-frequency representations, characterizes when and how strongly experimental conditions are represented in multivariate EEG activity via backward decoding models (BDM), and reconstructs the continuous, graded representational geometry underlying spatial attention via forward encoding models using channel tuning functions (CTF). The toolbox standardizes data organization, batch processing, and automated quality-control reporting across all four modules, supporting reproducible analysis pipelines from raw data through group-level statistics. We demonstrate OpenDvM's functionality on an openly shared EEG dataset probing multiple facets of attentional selection, including feature-based selection, spatial attention, and distractor suppression, and provide ten accompanying Jupyter notebook tutorials covering both core and advanced functionality. By lowering the barrier to combining these complementary analytical perspectives, OpenDvM aims to make integrated univariate and multivariate EEG analysis more accessible to researchers without extensive programming backgrounds.

articles_hidden.title: Hurricane Preparedness at the Crossroads of Objective Risk:  A Machine Learning Approach
articles_hidden.authors: Soheil Shapouri; Sudipto Banerjee; Roxane Cohen Silver; E. Alison Holman; Kayley Danielle Estes; Dana Rose Garfin
articles_hidden.abstract: Hurricane preparedness saves lives and reduces economic impacts, especially in United States Gulf Coast states, where climate change is intensifying disaster risk. articles_hidden.title: mstsa: A Python Library for Information-Theoretic and Statistical Analysis of EEG Microstate Sequences
articles_hidden.authors: FREDERIC VON WEGNER
articles_hidden.abstract:
EEG microstate analysis decomposes a multichannel EEG recording into a discrete symbolic time series: each sample is assigned to one of a small number of voltage topography templates, the microstate maps, typically at sampling rates of 100–500 Hz (Lehmann et al., 1998; Michel & Koenig, 2018; Pascual-Marqui et al., 1995). Back-fitting the templates into the original EEG dataset yields a symbolic time series, the microstate sequence. Many research questions address the temporal structure of these sequences, such as: time series memory (Markovianity), autocorrelations including persistence and long-range correlations, measures of syntax and complexity, and comparison against certain null models.
mstsa (Microstate Time Series Analysis) is a Python library that addresses these questions. It provides a comprehensive set of information-theoretic, Markov-chain, and statistical tools for the analysis of discrete symbolic sequences, with EEG microstate data as the primary application.

articles_hidden.title: Working With Circular Data: A Tutorial for Cognitive and Behavioral Research
articles_hidden.authors: Stella Wernicke; Julie de Falco; Zahara Gironés; Chris Jungerius; Ivan Tomic; Adam Triabhall; Xiaolu Wang; Paul Bays
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introductory statistics courses and conventional methods in behavioral and cognitive science are typically restricted to Euclidean space without explicitly stating this, leaving many researchers unaware of how to handle data with circular or periodic properties (e.g., time of day or orientation on a screen). This tutorial provides an accessible yet rigorous introduction, designed to bridge the gap between statistical theory and practical application. After an overview of common applications, we discuss different ways of representing circular data mathematically and fundamental principles for working with them. We explain angular and vector representations and operations, including key considerations for implementing them in computer code. We then survey methods for visualizing circular data, including linear and polar plots and presentation of summary statistics. Next, we discuss circular measures of central tendency, dispersion, and shape: how they relate to their Euclidean counterparts and why they differ. Finally, we turn to more advanced topics of the kind needed to construct models of circular data. We introduce the most common circular distribution families, including circular analogs of the Gaussian distribution and their properties, as well as flexible distribution families that can describe skewed and heavy-tailed data. The tutorial takes a method-oriented approach, not tied to specific software, but highlighting factors relevant to experimental design, data analysis, and statistical modeling. A consistent theme is the need to rigorously account for the inherent periodicity of circular data. We also provide a consistent notation for circular statistics and parameters, addressing the lack of established conventions in the field.

articles_hidden.title: Mechanistic Interpretability Needs a Logic of Inference
articles_hidden.authors: Zhimin Hu; Chen Jiang; Hanbo Xie; N Apurva Ratan Murty; Sashank Varma
articles_hidden.abstract: Neural networks are increasingly studied not merely as predictive systems, but as complex systems whose internal computations are themselves objects of scientific inquiry. Recent progress in mechanistic interpretability (MI) has made it possible to identify neurons, features, circuits, population structures, and dynamical patterns associated with model behavior. As these tools improve, attention is shifting from what can be observed inside a model to how those observations support mechanistic explanations. We examine the parallel efforts of neuroscience and MI to address this question and identify recurring inferential bottlenecks when inferring mechanisms from complex neural systems. Evidence beyond MI is ultimately required to establish what model mechanisms reveal about the world.

articles_hidden.title: Integrating eye-tracking and first-person interviews to link individual differences in gaze and subjective decision structure
articles_hidden.authors: Nicolas Bassan; Alain Finkel; Jean Jeuvrey; Françoise Jamen; Antoine Coutrot
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans have idiosyncratic and stable eye-scanning tendencies when exploring visual scenes. For instance, the gaze of participants who were more emotionally engaged was more driven by bottom-up visual saliency, and was more scattered across their preferred image. Our method uses the idiosyncrasy of gaze patterns as a structured signal reflecting personal decision process. articles_hidden.title: Evolution of occupational gender stereotypes over time and age
articles_hidden.authors: Laia Marcet; Ferran Pons
articles_hidden.abstract: Occupational gender stereotypes are widely held beliefs about which jobs are typically performed by men or women. However, there seems to be a delay between these societal changes and their effect on occupational gender stereotypes. In addition, age-related differences were observed, with older participants providing less stereotyped responses than younger participants. These differences were more pronounced for traditionally male-stereotyped occupations than for female-stereotyped ones. Potential causes for these a priori counterintuitive results will be explored and discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Assessing the reliability of hippocampal single-voxel proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy through intra-class effect decomposition

articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
The hippocampus is crucial for learning, memory, and stress regulation but is vulnerable to biological and environmental influences that compromise its structural and metabolic integrity. Proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) enables in vivo quantification of hippocampal neurochemistry, yet the absolute and relative reliability of these measures has rarely been systematically evaluated.
Methods
We assessed absolute and relative reliability in hippocampal metabolite estimates acquired with single-voxel MRS using a semi-adiabatic localization by adiabatic selective refocusing (semi-LASER) sequence at 3 T. Nineteen healthy adults (8 male; mean age = 40.9 ± 16.9 years) underwent four measurements across two consecutive days, with one session including an extended acquisition.
