Results
Despite high absolute reliability (CVs ≈ 4–7%), ICED indicated that relative reliability was generally poor to fair, with only myo-inositol, total choline, and total creatine reaching good intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs; 0.60–0.70). Increasing the number of transients improved spectral precision, reflected in higher signal-to-noise ratio and lower Cramér–Rao lower bounds, but did not enhance relative reliability.
Conclusions
Hippocampal metabolite quantification at 3 T showed high absolute but limited relative reliability, indicating that improved signal precision does not guarantee higher relative reliability. These findings highlight the need for methodological refinement, including automated voxel placement and advanced shimming, to improve the suitability of hippocampal MRS for longitudinal and individual-difference research.

articles_hidden.title: Umbrella Review and Evidence Map of Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Risk Factors for Early-Onset Bipolar Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Logan Thomas Smith; Cristian Alcaino; Kayla L. Baresich; Olivia C. Bishop; Mackenzie A. Maddox; Victoria Murphy; Robin Nusslock; Eric A. Youngstrom; Lauren Alloy
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: To synthesize systematic-review evidence on risk factors for early-onset bipolar disorder (EOBD), appraise methodological quality, assess factor-specific certainty, and map the evidence base.

Method: We conducted a PRISMA-compliant, PROSPERO-registered umbrella review of English-language systematic reviews and meta-analyses indexed in MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Embase, and the Cochrane Library before April 2026. EOBD was defined as bipolar disorder (BD) with a mean age at onset below 25 years in relevant primary studies. Review methods were appraised with AMSTAR-2; certainty for each risk-factor association was evaluated using an adapted GRADE framework. Findings were synthesized narratively and mapped by risk-factor type.

Results: Fifty-three reviews, including 20 meta-analyses, contributed evidence across 17 risk-factor categories. Family history of BD and ADHD diagnosis had moderate-certainty evidence. Parental age, depressive disorders, and sleep or circadian disturbances had low-certainty evidence; the remaining categories had very-low-certainty evidence. No factor reached high certainty. AMSTAR-2 ratings were predominantly low: 2 reviews were high, 16 moderate, 30 low, and 5 critically low. The evidence was uneven, geographically concentrated in Western populations, and partly dependent on recurring high-risk cohorts.

Conclusions: EOBD risk appears developmental, probabilistic, and multivariable. Family history of BD and ADHD diagnosis provide the strongest risk enrichment but are neither deterministic nor diagnostically specific. Future research should prioritize prospective, externally validated multivariable models; clinical application may favor staged longitudinal assessment rather than diagnosis or treatment based on any single marker. Policies could support tiered early-detection pathways, timely specialist access, and continuity across child and adult services without promoting risk-based labeling.

articles_hidden.title: Effects of an App to Support Managers of Autistic Employees:  A Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial
articles_hidden.authors: Marc J Lanovaz; Valerie Martin; Marie-Michèle Dufour; Elise Douard
articles_hidden.abstract: Purpose: Autistic individuals have employment rates significantly lower than individuals without a disability. One solution to this issue involves providing better support for managers who integrate autistic employees into their team. The purpose of our study was to examine the effects of a mobile app designed to support managers of autistic employees (i.e., My Autistic Employee). Methods: We compared attitudes, knowledge, and openness toward autism in 46 managers within a randomized controlled trial and measured their satisfaction with the mobile app. Results: Our results indicated that using the app improved knowledge of autism, but had no effect on the attitudes and openness of managers toward autistic employees. Furthermore, the participants reported being highly satisfied with the app. Our control group already had positive attitudes and high openness, which may explain part of the results. Conclusion: Replicating the study with a more representative sample appears essential to further establish the utility of the app.

articles_hidden.title: Dense-Sampling the Menstrual Cycle Using EEG in a Single Case Study: Relating Markers of Cognitive Control and Mental Health
articles_hidden.authors: Anne Nijboer; Federica Lucchi; Erik J. Giltay; Peter Putman; Ellen de Bruijn
articles_hidden.abstract: Introduction. Women may show menstrual cycle-related susceptibility to depressive and anxiety symptoms during estradiol (E2) and progesterone (P4) fluctuations. Electrophysiological (EEG) markers, including the error-related negativity (ERN) and resting-state theta/beta ratio (TBR) index cognitive control processes and are emerging biomarkers of adverse mental health outcomes. Methods. Using a proof-of-principle, hypothesis-generating approach, we intensively tracked one healthy, naturally cycling woman in her late twenties for 30 days. We collected daily salivary E2 and P4, mental health data, and EEG. We provide a descriptive case study to showcase a dense-sampling and dynamic time warping (DTW) combination. Results. EEG markers varied considerably across the menstrual cycle. The ERN was larger around ovulation, coinciding with an E2 peak. Around midluteal phase the ERN was smaller, coinciding with a P4 peak. TBR varied most during the early-follicular phase. The DTW networks suggested the ERN was related to TBR, that TBR was related to positive and negative affect, and to response bias on a Go/No-Go task.  Discussion. Our descriptive, hypothesis-generating results suggest that cognitive control markers can vary across a menstrual cycle, and that they can be important targets for further study regarding women’s mental health and precision medicine. Cognitive control markers exhibited considerable daily variability, underscoring the importance of accounting for such fluctuations in research.

articles_hidden.title: FEED your mind: The evolutionary roots of human food cognition
articles_hidden.authors: Camille Rioux; Raffaella I Rumiati; Annie E. Wertz; Carol Coricelli
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on food cognition has largely overlooked that our modern food environment strongly differs from the environment in which our ancestors lived. When foraging for food in wild environments, our ancestors had to distinguish edible food resources from myriad inedible and potentially toxic entities. In contrast, in most cultures today, many decisions about food are made during a trip to the grocery store or a meal at a restaurant, where we might ask ourselves: Is this item healthy? but certainly not: Is this item edible or poisonous? Here we argue that the scope of the problem humans faced with respect to food included navigating through wild environments to Find candidate food items, Excluding the costs of making a mistake and consuming a harmful food item, Evaluating the nutritional benefits of the potential foods and Deciding which food items to include in their diet. We call this the FEED problem and argue that it provides an organizing framework for thinking about the wide array of cognitive processes involved in human food psychology. The FEED problem can also be used as a generative theory to produce new testable empirical predictions about what cognitive mechanisms drive our modern food behaviors and provides a roadmap for future research in the field of food cognition.

articles_hidden.title: Assessing Lifetime Stressor Exposure Using the Stress and Adversity Inventory for Adults (Adult STRAIN) in Slovak: An Age- and Gender-Representative Sample
articles_hidden.authors: Jakub Rajcani; Annamária Antalová; Jana Martakova; Josef Hamza; Zach Gray; George M. Slavich
articles_hidden.abstract: Stress is widely recognized as a strong risk factor for developing both somatic and mental health problems. Although the cumulative impact of stress over the lifetime (i.e., allostatic load) has been measured for years based on biological indicators, a psychological measure of lifetime stressor exposure has been lacking. The Stress and Adversity Inventory (STRAIN) addresses this gap by assessing lifetime stressor exposure in an online, interview-based format. Here, we present the first validation of the Adult STRAIN into Slovak, conducted on a quota-based sample based on age and gender. A total of 260 participants, aged 18 to 85 years old, completed the STRAIN and a battery of questionnaires. Participants experienced 16.06 stressors, on average, with women experiencing more lifetime stressors. The STRAIN had high convergent validity as evidenced by associations with adverse childhood experiences, negative life events, and perceived stress. The STRAIN also exhibited excellent predictive utility in relation to self-reported physical (r = 0.30) and psychopathological symptoms (r = 0.33), sleep disturbance (r = 0.30), and doctor-diagnosed general health problems (OR = 1.043), autoimmune disorders (OR = 1.065) and psychiatric disorders (OR = 1.033) . Finally, the STRAIN exhibited no or very weak correlations with social desirability and participants’ personality traits, underscoring its discriminant validity. The Slovak STRAIN is thus a valid tool for assessing lifetime stressor exposure.

articles_hidden.title: Afraid of Hunger, Ashamed of Fullness: The Development and Validation of the Negative Appraisal of Gastric Sensations (NAGS) Scale and its association with Disordered Eating
articles_hidden.authors: Lucy Stafford; Anna Crossland; Alexandra Claire Pike; Catherine Preston
articles_hidden.abstract: Interoceptive dysfunction is central to eating disorders, and emerging evidence indicates that the maladaptive appraisal of gastrointestinal signals predicts pathology better than body-general interoception. However, existing tools do not adequately measure this construct; they conflate sensation intensity with appraisal and assess a limited range of emotional responses, likely due to little input from eating disorder populations during tool development. To address this gap, we developed and validated the Negative Appraisal of Gastric Sensations (NAGS) scale to specifically capture the affective interpretation of hunger and fullness. Exploratory factor analysis (sample 1 n=337, 80.12% Female, 75.97% White British) and confirmatory factor analysis (sample 2 n=337, 85.16% Female, 79.23% White British) supported a two-factor scale: hunger-fear and fullness-shame. The scale demonstrated robust psychometric properties, including strong internal and test-retest reliability, as well as criterion, concurrent, convergent, and discriminant validity. The subscales successfully distinguished eating disorder from gastrointestinal disorder and non-disordered controls, and this was not attributable to differential item functioning. Exploratory analyses using latent profile analysis and hierarchical regressions supported the measure’s utility as a critical interoceptive factor in eating disorders over and above existing interoceptive measures: increases in fullness-shame predicted higher overall symptom severity, body dissatisfaction, and purge-only category membership, while increases in hunger-fear specifically predicted restriction-only category membership. As such, the scale could be considered a useful tool for researchers studying the somatic experience of eating disorders, but also primary care physicians for distinguishing primary gastrointestinal disorders from eating disorders presenting as gastrointestinal complaints.

articles_hidden.title: Fluently Grooving: Investigating neural and behavioural indices of processing fluency in complex auditory rhythms
articles_hidden.authors: Christian Dyhre Foldal; Jonna Katariina Vuoskoski
articles_hidden.abstract: The internal representation and prediction of temporal regularities are central processes in music listening. Processing fluency – the ease with which sensory input is perceptually organized – is thought to drive rhythm-evoked pleasure and the desire to move, which may arise via predictive mechanisms. It remains unclear, however, whether fluency can be actively facilitated in rhythmically complex music, and which psychophysiological signals index it: cortical tracking of external periodicities, or motor-supported internal beat representation. We tested whether processing fluency of complex polymetric rhythms increases with a metrical prior (Prime; accented count-in) or enhanced beat salience (Pulse; superimposed accents). While 42 participants listened to polymetric drum grooves, we measured electroencephalography (EEG; neural entrainment and sensorimotor beta/mu desynchronization), facial electromyography (EMG; zygomaticus major and corrugator supercilii), and ratings of beat strength, pleasure, desire to move, and complexity. Pulse significantly enhanced perceived beat strength, pleasure, and the desire to move without affecting complexity, while Prime did not yield any significant effects on the neural or subjective measures. Beta- and mu-desynchronization – but not neural entrainment – were significantly associated with subjective ratings: beta-desynchronization tracked pleasure, desire to move, and beat strength, whereas mu-desynchronization related more selectively to the desire to move and to lower perceived complexity. Corrugator activity was associated with reduced pleasure, desire to move, and beat strength, while zygomaticus activity showed no reliable associations. These findings suggest that subjective fluency emerges not simply from resonance with external periodicities, but from the stability of internally generated beat representations supported by motor system involvement.

articles_hidden.title: From brain networks to the patient-environment system in clinical neuroimaging
articles_hidden.authors: david corredor; Maxime Carriere; Anaïs Vallet; MELINA GASTELUM; Vicente Raja; Francis Eustache; berengere guillery
articles_hidden.abstract:
Despite substantial advances in clinical neuroimaging, its impact on defining and treating
psychiatric disorders remains limited. Current approaches in clinical brain imaging frame
psychiatric disorders as dysfunctions of brain-based information processing. Here, we
propose a shift in this explanatory focus, from how aberrant neural processes generate
maladaptive behavior to the brain's participation in the dynamics of the patient–
environment system. Drawing on organism-environment approaches, we conceptualize
behavior as emerging from context-dependent coordinated interactions among brain,
body, and environment. Within this framework, we conceptualize psychiatric disorders
as excessive stability or flexibility in patient-environment dynamics that impair the
patient's capacity to adapt to changing situations. After examining the ontological
commitments of current clinical neuroimaging and recasting psychiatric disorders in
terms of patient–environment dynamics, we outline concrete strategies for
operationalizing this framework. These progress from combining ecological momentary
assessment with neuroimaging, to naturalistic brain and body imaging that jointly tracks
neural, bodily, and environmental dynamics, and finally to explicit dynamical models of
the patient–environment system in which maladaptive stability or flexibility can be
formally defined and identified. By making these dynamics measurable, we aim to turn a
conceptual reframing into a concrete empirical program, recasting the brain not as the
seat of psychiatric disorders but as one participant in the patient–environment dynamics.

articles_hidden.title: The cost of saying no: behavioural, physiological, motor, and agency-related responses to corruption under threat in immersive virtual reality
articles_hidden.authors: Alisha Vabba; Matteo P. Lisi; Salvatore Maria Aglioti
articles_hidden.abstract: Corruption can involve not only incentives to comply, but also personal costs for refusing. This combination of reward and threat is especially relevant in forms of coercive corruption, including organised-crime contexts in which bribery and intimidation may operate together. To investigate the psychological processes underlying these decisions, we developed an immersive virtual reality (IVR) economic game in which participants acted as public officials responsible for awarding government contracts. Virtual agents repeatedly offered bribes in exchange for preferential treatment. Accepting a bribe benefited the participant financially but imposed either a monetary loss or a mild electric shock on a third party. In some trials, refusing the bribe also exposed participants to the risk of receiving a mild electric shock themselves, allowing us to experimentally manipulate the personal cost of refusal. We examined how threat and the type of negative externality influenced corrupt decisions, autonomic arousal, motor conflict, and sense of agency. Participants were more likely to accept bribes under threat, and acceptance was also more likely when the consequence for the third party was monetary rather than physical. Threat increased skin conductance responses, particularly when participants refused, and delayed movement initiation, suggesting that coercive pressure affected both anticipatory arousal and action preparation. Measures of sense of agency showed a more complex pattern than predicted, with no evidence that threat produced the reduction in agency typically observed in direct-coercion paradigms. Together, these findings show that IVR can be used to study coercive corruption in an ecologically richer but experimentally controlled setting, while also capturing behavioural, physiological, motor, and agency-related processes that unfold during corrupt decision-making.

articles_hidden.title: The Benefits of and Motivations Behind Large-Team Coordination in Psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Sajedeh Rasti; Krist Vaesen; Daniel Lakens
articles_hidden.abstract: To increase coordination in science in areas where this would be beneficial for knowledge generation, collaborative work needs to offer clear benefits to individual researchers. This study investigates the motivations for initiating large-team papers and the potential benefits of these projects in psychology. By qualitatively analyzing 500 papers, we find that large-team collaborations are most often instigated to deal with the practical challenges  inherent to complex research questions, but can also be motivated by broader social and or strategic factors. The results from quantitatively analyzing 1,699,513 papers published between 1975 and 2024 indicate that large-team collaborations are more likely to be cited and to appear in higher-ranked journals. Furthermore, their immediate impact on the field, as measured by citation counts within the first 2 years after publication, is on average higher than individually-authored papers. This suggests that contributing to collaborative projects in psychology will likely increase the number of high-rank journal publications to the resume of researchers. Overall, our findings indicate that large-team collaborations can be rewarding for individual researchers both by enabling early scientific impact and by contributing to stronger publication records.

articles_hidden.title: Including social network quality in public health research: a scoping review on current practices
articles_hidden.authors: Rik Crutzen; Senne Maria Catharina Elisabeth Wijnen; Karoline Huth; Florian van Daalen; Nicole Dukers-Muijrers; Lisanne Catharina Johanna Steijvers
articles_hidden.abstract:
Aim: To (1) provide insight into how social network quality can be included in public health research and (2) generate directions for future research concerning the conceptualization and measurement of social network quality. 

Methods: A pre-registered scoping review using PubMed and APA PsychInfo as information sources. Sources of evidence were deemed eligible if they were full-text articles and reported on conceptualization and/or measurement of social network quality in public health research concerning humans. 

Results: In total, 78 articles were included. For most articles, the possible conceptualization used (if any) could only be implied based on the aspects that are measured in the reported studies. There is a large heterogeneity in aspects, with some recurring frequently (e.g., support, specific relationships, and satisfaction). This is indicative of differences in researchers’ conceptualization of social network quality.

Conclusion: The point of departure for future research is to advance the conceptualization of social network quality. The diversity in current conceptualizations and measurements of social network quality in public health research can even be beneficial. However, to benefit from this epistemic diversity, researchers need to make their conceptualizations and measurements explicit – and share them with others.

articles_hidden.title: Online Platforms Provide Access to Valid Eastern Samples
articles_hidden.authors: Liman Wang; Randy Gao; Minah H. Jung; Iris W. Hung; Leif D. Nelson
articles_hidden.abstract: Behavioral scientists make claims about humans, but most research relies on English-speaking Americans. Despite longstanding concerns about this narrow sampling, only limited progress has been made to address it. We evaluated Chinese online participant pools, a potentially valuable resource given China’s large population, global influence, and frequent comparison with Western societies. Across 16 preregistered studies covering 21 established phenomena from behavioral and cultural sciences, we collected data from 24,932 Chinese and American participants. Chinese online platforms produced data broadly comparable to established American platforms. Participants were geographically and demographically diverse, attentive, and showed high test–retest reliability and temporal stability. Psychological and cultural effects were robust to variation in translation and translator backgrounds. We also provide practical insights and guidance for researchers using Chinese online platforms. This work helps reduce logistical barriers to extending behavioral research beyond traditionally studied WEIRD populations.

articles_hidden.title: Grounding meaning in social and emotional experience: Challenges and opportunities
articles_hidden.authors: Pablo Solana
articles_hidden.abstract: Within the broader debate on how the mind and brain represent meaning, multiple representation theories have positioned social and emotional experience, along with their underlying neural systems, as key sources for concept grounding. In this article, I review the current evidence for this proposal and discuss several conceptual and methodological challenges, including the limited capacity of behavioral evidence to support this view, the difficulties associated with interpreting neuroimaging findings, the need for stronger causal evidence, and the importance of adopting open science practices. I argue that these limitations converge on a common concern: in their current form, many findings taken to support multiple representation theories of socio-affective grounding do not provide sufficiently diagnostic evidence to empirically adjudicate between them and competing accounts of semantic representation. In response, I outline a set of methodological recommendations and underexplored ideas that may help refine the theoretical framework, generate more decisive tests, and guide future research.

articles_hidden.title: A call for a mechanistic-neutral nomenclature replacing “neuromelanin-sensitive” imaging
articles_hidden.authors: Heidi I. L. Jacobs; Dorothea Hämmerer; Mara Mather; Benedikt A Poser; James Rowe
articles_hidden.abstract:
The locus coeruleus (LC) and substantia nigra (SN) have attracted attention in the search for early biomarkers and new therapeutic targets in neurodegenerative and psychiatric diseases. MRI methods that provide contrast in the LC and SN are commonly described as “neuromelanin-sensitive.” This terminology originated from early observations linking the MRI signal topography to apparent spatial correspondence with pigmented regions at autopsy. 

However, converging evidence from MRI physics, modelling, and animal studies indicates that the observed contrast cannot be attributed specifically to neuromelanin. Instead, it reflects a complex interplay of different MRI physical properties that can yield diverse biological interpretations depending on the context, age, region, and disease. Continued use of the term therefore risks conflating MRI measurement properties with biological interpretation, leading to overattributing MRI-signal changes to neuromelanin accumulation and loss across the lifespan and with disease. 

We argue that the term “neuromelanin-sensitive” should be abandoned, and propose instead a descriptive reporting framework with terminology that separates acquisition (“type”), the visible signal (“contrast”), quantification (“derivative”), and biological interpretation (“inference”). This new approach will improve interpretability, comparability, and conceptual rigor in locus coeruleus and substantia nigra research.

articles_hidden.title: Music influences the content of spontaneous thought
articles_hidden.authors: Wei Wu; Elizabeth Hellmuth Margulis; Kelly Jakubowski
articles_hidden.abstract: Spontaneous thought is a form of cognition that is relatively unconstrained and free flowing. Recent accounts have raised the possibility that the generation and content of spontaneous thought can be influenced by even weak perceptual constraints. We leveraged this perspective to develop an approach using music, a ubiquitous stimulus that permeates our everyday environments, as a window into the mechanisms that shape spontaneous thought content. Adults spanning four age groups listened to music from ten different genres and completed the open-ended task of writing descriptions of any thoughts that arose. Natural language processing analysis was applied to obtain computational similarity (word2vec) of the semantic meaning of thought descriptions. We found that thoughts sustained while hearing music from the same genre shared greater semantic similarity than those sustained while hearing music from different genres, and participants from the same age group experienced more similar thoughts than those from different age groups. Properties that varied naturally with genre, including the music’s auditory features, expressed emotions, and contextual associations, all contributed significantly to explaining the greater semantic similarity of thoughts within genres. These results demonstrate that spontaneous thought can be jointly shaped by perceptual and experiential constraints, opening new avenues for understanding when and why particular thoughts come to mind, with implications for creativity and mental health.

articles_hidden.title: Personal Rhythms of Memory: Investigating Individual Effects of Preferred Theta Phase Lag between Sensory Inputs on Associative Memory
articles_hidden.authors: Fatih Serin; Benedikt Zoefel; Matthew H. Davis; Richard Henson
articles_hidden.abstract: Episodic memory formation requires integrating multisensory information. Inspired by animal research on how hippocampal theta oscillations modulate long-term potentiation, recent human studies have demonstrated that memory for auditory and visual stimuli modulated synchronously at theta frequency (4 Hz) is better than when those stimuli are modulated asynchronously; the so-called Theta-Induced Memory Enhancement (TIME) effect. However, recent failures to replicate the TIME effect question its robustness and dependence on other variables. One such variable may be inter-individual differences in neural sensitivity to the precise phase lag between auditory and visual streams. In this online study, we therefore tested a wider range of phase lags between 4 Hz modulated audio and visual stimuli. Using simulation methods from Zoefel et al. (2019), we estimated the sample size to achieve 90% statistical power to detect an optimal phase lag that varied across participants. However, this sample size showed no evidence that some phase lags produced better performance than others, thereby failing to replicate the TIME effect regardless of whether or not the optimal lag was assumed to vary across participants. Indeed, Bayes Factors supported the null for most analyses, and a follow-up analysis showed no evidence that the TIME effect depended on overall memory performance. Therefore, the present work adds to the growing number of non-replications of the TIME effect, though the reason for these failures remains unclear.

articles_hidden.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis on motion sensitivity in schizophrenia
articles_hidden.authors: Antonio González-Del Pozo; Cristina de la Malla; Daniel Linares
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Altered performance in visual perception tasks is well documented in schizophrenia and may offer insight into the neural and computational dysfunction underlying the disorder. Motion perception is among the most extensively studied visual domains, yet it has not been systematically reviewed and meta-analyzed. It therefore remains unclear whether motion sensitivity is robustly impaired in schizophrenia, how large the deficit is, whether it depends on antipsychotic medication, and to what extent it may reflect attentional lapses.

Methods: Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched for studies measuring motion sensitivity in individuals with schizophrenia and healthy controls. We calculated Hedges’ g for each experimental condition reported within each study (e.g., measuring sensitivity across different stimulus sizes or speeds) and pooled effect sizes using a three-level random-effects meta-analysis.

Results: Across 41 studies (88 effect sizes), patients showed a robust, medium-magnitude deficit in motion-sensitivity (g = 0.59, 95% CI from 0.49 to 0.68, P = 2.7 x 10-20). The deficit was present for both direction and speed discrimination, though task requirements were strongly confounded with stimulus type. We found no evidence that the deficit depended on antipsychotic medication. In the three studies manipulating stimulus size, the deficit was larger for small than large stimuli, consistent with reduced spatial suppression. Evidence did not clearly support a deficit specific to global motion integration. Only two studies estimated attentional lapse rates.

Conclusions: Schizophrenia is associated with a robust deficit in motion sensitivity, with no evidence of dependence on antipsychotic medication. Future studies should systematically account for attentional lapses to determine how much of the observed deficit reflects genuine perceptual impairment. Disentangling task and stimulus parameters, together with systematic manipulation of stimulus size, may help clarify the mechanisms underlying the deficit, including potential alterations in spatial suppression and integration.

articles_hidden.title: Is Sexual Orientation Diversity Overlooked in Autism Research? Examining If and How Sexual Orientation Is Considered in Australian Autism Research
articles_hidden.authors: Robin Michiels; Sophie Hindes; Megan Walsh; Timea Molnar; Halle Wiblen; Simon Bury; Dawn Adams
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose: Sexual orientation is an important aspect of diversity in the Autistic population, yet how and how often it is reported in autism research remains unclear. 
Methods: This brief report examined the reporting of sexual orientation minority status in Australian autism research published 2023-25. Conclusion: Sexual orientation remains underreported and underanalysed in autism research. Recommendations for more transparent, inclusive, and analytically meaningful research practices are provided.

articles_hidden.title: Neural responses to conditioned threat during extinction predict concurrent and future anxiety in late adolescence
articles_hidden.authors: Kubra Ulusoy; Liat Levita
articles_hidden.abstract: Adolescence is a critical developmental period characterised by heightened anxiety and increased risk for anxiety disorders, potentially reflecting developmental differences in threat learning and extinction processes. Although previous research suggests that early adolescents show enhanced visual event-related potential (ERP) responses to conditioned threat cues, it remains unclear whether these neural patterns persist into late adolescence or predict anxiety vulnerability. This study examined neural responses to conditioned threat cues during threat acquisition and extinction in late adolescence and investigated their association with current and future anxiety. Sixty-eight late adolescents (aged 18-19) completed a Pavlovian threat conditioning task in which a conditioned stimulus (CS+) was paired with an aversive sound on 50% of trials, whereas a second cue (CS-) was never reinforced. An immediate extinction phase followed, during which both cues were presented without reinforcement. Behavioural and physiological measures indicated successful threat acquisition and extinction. ERP analyses revealed no evidence of differential conditioning in P1 amplitudes. In contrast, N1 amplitudes were significantly larger to the CS- than the CS+ across both acquisition and extinction. The late positive potential (LPP) showed the opposite pattern, with larger amplitudes to the CS+ than the CS- during both phases. Logistic regression analyses controlling for depressive symptoms and gender indicated that P1 and N1 responses were unrelated to current or future anxiety caseness. Whereas greater LPP differentiation (CS+ > CS-) during extinction was associated with increased odds of belonging to the high-anxiety group both concurrently and six months later. Together, these findings suggest that differences between high- and low-anxiety adolescents are reflected in later neural responses to conditioned threat during extinction, but not in early visual sensory-attentional processing. Extinction-related LPP responses may therefore represent a promising neural marker of current and future anxiety in late adolescence.

articles_hidden.title: Testing the prevalent consistency assumption of (un)conscious processing through massive feature extraction of inattentional blindness electroencephalography
articles_hidden.authors: Angus Leung; Yota Kawashima; Naotsugu Tsuchiya
articles_hidden.abstract: Freud’s iceberg metaphor has long been used to describe (un)consciousness: a huge unconsciousness supports a tiny tip of consciousness. Inspired by this, research has assumed that unconscious discriminative processing persists into consciousness, employing contrastive analysis to isolate the neural correlates of consciousness (NCC). For example, in electroencephalography (EEG) studies, features of time series are related to unconscious sensory processes if they discriminate presence of invisible visual stimuli. According to the consistency assumption, they should also discriminate these stimuli when they become visible and task relevant. Despite its prevalence, the assumption has never been directly questioned, and its general validity for EEG studies, regardless of the exact analysis method employed, is unclear. This registered report aims to explicitly test this assumption by utilising a toolbox providing over 7000 time-series features from various analysis methods from a wide range of research fields. We apply these features to an inattentional blindness paradigm and identify features which discriminate presence of a visual stimulus which is initially invisible, and then later visible and task relevant. We track the performance of each feature in discriminating the presence of the stimulus as it varies in visibility, and use a Bayesian framework to test whether the consistency assumption is likely to be valid. Pilot results suggest it is likely invalid across the range of time-series features.

articles_hidden.title: Profiling the Chinese Participants in Psychological Science: Non-WEIRD but Not Representative
articles_hidden.authors: Lei Yue; Zhangweiwei; Chunxiao Wang; Xi-Nian Zuo; Hu Chuan-Peng
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychological science aims at understanding the human mind and behavior, but it primarily relies on participants from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic regions, i.e., the WEIRD problem. This lack of diversity and representativeness of participants compromises the generalizability of psychological science. To address this issue, large-scale international collaborative projects have been initiated, and more data have been collected from non-WEIRD regions. However, it is unknown whether participants from non-WEIRD regions can represent their local population. In this preregistered report, we depicted the demographic profile of Chinese participants reported in 1, 000 empirical studies (n = 554, 794) published in five mainstream Chinese psychological journals and in 27 large-scale international collaborative projects (n = 29, 006, accounting for 2.12% of all participants). We found that age and sex were the most reported demographic variables, and other aspects of participants were less reported. The available demographic information revealed that Chinese participants were not representative of the population: most were young, well-educated, and resided in East China. Also, Chinese participants in large-scale international collaborative projects are less representative than those from Chinese journals in terms of geographical distributions. The demographic profile of Chinese participants in psychology is similar to their counterparts in many other countries and regions, suggesting the globalization of young and highly educated participants in psychological science. Together, our findings indicate that problems of representativeness are deeply entrenched in global psychological science and require coordinated cross-sector efforts.

articles.title: Co-creating change in agriculture and food systems: A systematic review of co-creation processes and approaches for evaluating their contributions to sustainability transformation
articles.authors: Sara Delaney; Sophia Alami; Maria Busse; Bonnie Averbuch; Fanny Boeraeve; Pauline Cassart; Valéria Csonka; Graeme Dean; Cedric Gossart; Bienvenu Kambashi
articles.abstract:
Co-creation is widely proposed to address complex sustainability challenges by bringing together diverse forms of experience and expertise. Yet practical, evidence-based guidance on how co-creation processes can support sustainability transformation remains fragmented and insufficient, including for agriculture and food systems. We conducted a systematic literature review to characterize scholarly work on co-creation for environmental sustainability and to identify process insights relevant to Living Labs and related participatory initiatives. Following a four-stage screening procedure, we reviewed 5,291 articles and retained 266 studies describing multi-stakeholder, action-oriented, experimental processes; 51 agriculture- and food-focused articles were subjected to in-depth qualitative analysis. We combined bibliometric and descriptive analyses, including co-authorship network mapping, with framework-guided qualitative coding of co-creation inputs, processes, outcomes, impacts, and evaluation practices.
Publications on this topic increased substantially over the past decade, but relatively few studies documented action and experimentation in sufficient methodological detail. Agriculture and food studies constituted a moderately self-contained segment of the broader literature. Across the qualitative sample, five enabling factors were most consistently associated with productive co-creation: participant alignment, institutional support, strong facilitation, inclusive participation and trust, and sufficient time for iteration. Studies also identified recurring trade-offs between diversity and alignment, resource-intensive engagement and scalability, and place specificity and transferability. Frequently reported outcomes were new knowledge, communication and networks, empowerment or efficacy, and skills. However, evidence of longer-term sustainability impacts was limited: most articles described intermediate outcomes rather than demonstrated transformation. Only sixteen articles evaluated the co-creation process itself, and participatory development of evaluation criteria was rare. Co-creation efforts can build the practical and relational capacities, and “social infrastructure” needed for sustainability transitions, but stronger methodological reporting and participatory, longitudinal evaluation are needed for validation of criteria and proxies for impact and establishment of how these processes contribute to lasting transformation.

articles.title: Violence and International Migration in Illiberal Times: The Case of El Salvador’s Authoritarian Transformation
articles.authors: Jeffrey Swindle; Matthew Blanton
articles.abstract: Across a new transnational wave of illiberal governance, tough-on-crime approaches to public safety and migration are growing. The case of El Salvador, in which President Nayib Bukele suspended due process protections and imprisoned suspected gang members in mass beginning in late March 2022 under a State of Exception policy, offers a window into this process. Turning to a combination of administrative datasets and cross-national surveys, we show that despite tremendous public approval for President Bukele’s strategies as the solution to a long history of persistent gang violence and international migration, violence largely reduced before he implemented the State of Exception, and Salvadorans’ migration intentions have not declined. Moreover, we find no evidence that the policy or Bukele taking office produced a particular reduction in Salvadoran migration to either the U.S. or Mexico compared to Guatemalan and Honduran migration. Nor do we uncover clear evidence that return migration to El Salvador uniquely increased, undercutting conclusions that illiberal tough-on-crime policies like El Salvador’s are likely to address “root causes” of international migration.

articles.title: Generative AI and Society
articles.authors: Laura K. Nelson; Daniel Karell; Thomas Davidson
articles.abstract: For sociologists, generative AI inherits the legacy of earlier computational technologies: it is an advancement of machine learning already adopted as a methodology, and it intervenes in a society already shaped by algorithmic systems. Yet it also has a dimension that distinguishes it from previous computational methods, and one that makes it inherently sociological: its interactivity. In this review, we conceptualize the interactivity of generative AI and introduce a framework for understanding how it operates across individual, organizational, and institutional life. Specifically, the framework specifies how generative AI expands users, functions as a proxy for society, and expresses power, both in sociological practice and in society. We conclude by suggesting three dynamics driven by generative AI that sociology will face in the near future: the transformation of scientific practice, the reorganization of social interaction, and the acceleration of algorithmic governance.

articles.title: Able but unwilling? Mapping citizens’ political GenAI use through the lens of Expectancy-Value Theory
articles.authors: Michael van Straelen; Christopher Starke; Patrick van Erkel; Jessica Piotrowski; Nils Köbis
articles.abstract:
Generative AI (GenAI) holds promise and risk for democracy, yet little is known about how
citizens evaluate and adopt it for political purposes. Drawing on Expectancy-Value Theory
and Uses & Gratifications Theory, this study offers an initial account of political GenAI
adoption, mapping how citizens' cost-value perceptions and expectancy beliefs cluster into
distinct profiles. We investigate how these ‘expectancy-value profiles’ shape political GenAI
use. Using cross-sectional survey data from 947 Dutch respondents, we conduct a latent
profile analysis, identifying four profiles: optimists, cautious pragmatists, sceptics, and
indifferents. Profile differences stem largely from differing cost-value perceptions rather than
expectancy beliefs, suggesting the question is less about whether people feel able to use
GenAI, and more about whether they feel it is worth using. Across all profiles, cost
perceptions are high and political use is low, though optimists report significantly more use
than others. Individuals’ political dispositions predict usage but not profile membership and
among technological dispositions, trust in GenAI and belief in the machine heuristic predict
being an optimist. Findings raise concerns about uncalibrated trust among adopters.

articles.title: The Power of “We” in Science Funding and Publication
articles.authors: Lijian Peng; Wenwen Li; Yi Bu; Hao Peng
articles.abstract:
Linguistic communication supports all stages of scientific innovation. However, we have limited understanding of rhetorical strategies for facilitating the recognition of new ideas in science. 
Drawing on prior literature on the importance of personal pronouns in inter-personal communication, we examine the unique role of first-person plural pronouns (``We'' words, including ``we'', ``us'', ``our'') in science funding and publishing. 
Our study leverages the full sample of 13K grant proposals submitted to the Novo Nordisk Foundation and 47K research papers submitted to BMJO and ICLR between 2011 and 2024. 
We find a strong and universal positive association between ``we'' words and success rates even after accounting for important confounding factors related to content, novelty, and author impact.
Specifically, a one percentage point increase in the percentage of ``We'' words used in the full text is associated with a 36-51% increase in the odds of success for grants and papers.
Furthermore, we find that the effect of ``We'' is applicable to both editors and reviewers of BMJO papers that used the single-blind review and is predictive of more positive and engaging review feedback for ICLR papers that employed the double-blind review.
Crucially, a large-scale LLM-assisted computational experiment that replaces ``We'' words with demonstrative pronouns provides robust causal evidence of ``We'' words on paper acceptance.
Lastly, our causal mediation analysis shows that ``We'' words can lead to more acceptance mainly because they can increase the perceived teamwork, credibility, significance, and robustness in research evaluation.
By revealing the unique strength of ``We'' in facilitating the recognition of new ideas in science, our study highlights the importance of small but mighty linguistic choices in promoting knowledge discoveries and breakthroughs.

articles.title: Turning Votes into Power: New Women Voters and Access to Local Governance
articles.authors: Mirya Holman; Christina Wolbrecht; Lakshmi Iyer
articles.abstract: Do voting rights secure access to political power for previously excluded groups? We theorize that organizational capacity and ideological congruence with political regimes determine whether voting rights produce access to governance. We test this theory with the case of American women’s suffrage and a new measure of access to power: representation on local appointed boards. Using a new dataset of more than 30,000 appointees, hundreds of women’s organizations, and local political regimes in four major cities, we find that suffrage facilitates descriptive representation, but this connection is limited to when women are ideologically aligned with the political regime. Strength of women’s organizations is associated with women’s representation, but only before suffrage. Women’s representation remained concentrated on boards concerning children, arts, and welfare. Even with the vote, women’s access to governance depended on the preferences of the established male elite.

articles.title: Questionnaire Design and Rater Cognition in 360-Degree Performance Appraisal
articles.authors: Saber Mirzaei Ahandani; Simin Ebrahimi Lialekol
articles.abstract:
Questionnaire design may play an important yet underexamined role in shaping the quality of performance appraisal data. This study examines whether redesigning response formats in a 360-degree feedback system is associated with improvements in rating behavior, response quality, and psychometric consistency. Drawing on cognitive processing and response-process perspectives, we compare a traditional numeric Likert-format questionnaire with a redesigned format incorporating behaviorally descriptive response options, modified visual presentation, and variable response ordering.
Data were collected across two appraisal periods within a large production organization employing more than 25,000 individuals. A total of 26,672 questionnaires were distributed, and 18,621 responses were obtained for the evaluation of approximately 900 managers in different levels. Following the redesign, participation rates increased from 47% to 79%, and internal consistency reliability improved from Cronbach’s α = 0.902 to α = 0.939. Response distributions also became less concentrated in extreme categories and more evenly distributed across intermediate categories, indicating greater rating differentiation and reduced response bias.
These findings are consistent with the argument that behaviorally descriptive response formats encourage greater cognitive engagement and reduce reliance on heuristic responding during performance evaluation. The study contributes to performance appraisal and multisource feedback research by highlighting the role of questionnaire design in shaping response processes, rating behavior, and measurement quality. Together, the findings provide evidence compatible with the view that relatively small and scalable questionnaire design modifications may enhance cognitive engagement, improve measurement quality, and increase the validity and practical usefulness of organizational appraisal data.

articles.title: The Latent Interview Protocol: Recovering Enacted Question Structure for Large-Scale Interview Analysis
articles.authors: Zachary Lim
articles.abstract: Interview researchers increasingly work with large corpora for which traditional line-by-line coding is costly. Current proposed indexing strategies to make the corpus more manageable still require line-by-line indexing while assuming that the planned interview protocol accurately represents what was asked in practice. This article introduces the latent interview protocol—the recurring substantive questions that organize interviews as enacted, along with the pathways linking them—and LIPE, an open-source workflow that recovers this structure by combining sentence embeddings, density-based clustering, and researcher-guided refinement. Validated protocol questions are assembled into a corpus-level structure and used to retrieve local response blocks for downstream qualitative analysis. An application to 63 semi-structured interviews on mothering during COVID-19 shows that LIPE recovers most planned protocol questions, surfaces emergent lines of inquiry, and retrieves question-anchored responses with high precision and recall. The approach makes large-scale interview indexing more tractable while preserving interpretive control over analytic boundaries.

articles.title: Accessibility as Infrastructure: A Neurodivergent Led Model for Structural Communication Safety in Disability Support Systems
articles.authors: Neil McCarthy
articles.abstract:
Disabled people frequently experience communication collapse during distress, overwhelm or coercive control, producing indirect, fragmented, masked or delayed expression rather than clear verbal articulation. National Inquiries – including the Disability Royal Commission (2023) and the NDIS Review (2023) – demonstrate that current disability and safeguarding systems are misaligned with these communication realities, relying on speech, privacy, cognitive stability and narrative coherence at precisely the moments that these capacities fail. Communication Collapse is there a predictable, embodied response shaped by trauma, cognitive load and social misunderstanding, rather than and individual deficit.
This article introduces accessibility as infrastructure, a conceptual reframing that positions communication safety as a structural requirement of safeguarding systems. Drawing on disability studies and critical social theory, it argues that safeguarding infrastructures must be redesigned to recognise neurodivergent communication as valid and actionable, particularly during shutdown, overwhelm, masking, executive- function collapse and coercive control.
Within this framework, the article presents Althing, a neurodivergent-led, trauma informed safeguarding model engineered to remain usable during distress-state communication collapse. By supporting early, low-detail, indirect or delayed signals of harm, Althing addresses structural communication failures and aligns with national reform expectations for trauma-informed, low-demand safeguarding pathways. Although conceptual, the model offers a mature foundation, for future co-design, empirical evaluation, and state-level safeguarding innovation, demonstrating how accessibility as infrastructure can strengthen communication safety at the exact moments disabled people are least able to seek help.

articles.title: Jumping to Solutions? Bureaucratic Attention Allocation in Response to Negative Performance Feedback
articles.authors: Amandine Lerusse; Joris van der Voet; Wouter Lammers
articles.abstract: Attention allocation is fundamental for governance, policy-making and management in the public administration. The attention-based view highlights how informationally and cognitively constrained bureaucrats allocate their finite attention to diagnose performance shortfalls and identify potential solutions. This study informs bureaucratic attention allocation toward solution-generation and problem-definition using a multi-method approach that combines a laboratory eye-tracking experiment with vignette-based interviews among 41 bureaucrats. We find that bureaucrats process problem-related and solution-related information in sequence and allocate more attention to solution-generation than problem-definition. The interviews demonstrate how the bureaucratic decision context gives rise to role-based, substantive, strategic and aspirational justifications for these patterns in attention allocation. We offer important implications for public administration research, theory and practice, highlighting the ever-increasing demands on bureaucratic decision-makers’ scarce attentional resources.

articles.title: The effects of childhood family disruption on sexual attitudes, experiences and well-being
articles.authors: Yucheng He; Yao Ma; zhuofei lu
articles.abstract: More than 40% of children in the representative UK Millennium Cohort Study experienced a risk of family disruption (i.e., not living with both biological parents by age 14), a circumstance widely recognized as shaping the early developmental environment. Yet the longer-term implications of family disruption for offspring’s sexual attitudes, experiences, and sexual well-being remain surprisingly underexamined. Drawing on 10,624 respondents from the most recent wave (2010–2012) of Natsal-3, and combining weighted OLS and logistic regression models, this study yields several novel findings. First, individuals who experienced family disruption by age 14 face elevated risks of non-volitional sex. Family disruption is also associated with more permissive sexual norms and greater involvement in boundary-testing sexual practices. Moreover, it is linked to slightly poorer sexual functioning and more frequent symptoms of low sexual mood. Taken together, these results provide new evidence that childhood family disruption has enduring consequences for sexual attitudes, experiences, and sexual well-being, underscoring the need for greater attention to interventions supporting children who experience family disruption.

articles.title: Grensoverschrijdend bevoegdheidsvacuüm in de sociale zekerheid.
articles.authors: Eric Messa
articles.abstract: Empirische en kwantificeerbare systeem-audit van het grensoverschrijdend bevoegdheidsvacuüm in de sociale zekerheid tussen België en Nederland (Verordening EG 883/2004). Bevat forensische verslaglegging van meer dan 200 overheidsinteracties, deconstructie van de En/En-paradox en een concrete beleidssynthese met drie infrastructurele bouwstenen.

articles.title: Thoughtforms in the Fog: Liminal Warfare and the Defense of Human Agency
articles.authors: Michael Paul Ross
articles.abstract:
Cognitive warfare is commonly framed as a contest over perception and decision-making. This
article argues that its most consequential leverage often appears during liminal periods, when
established identities, meanings, and institutions no longer provide sufficient orientation. It
introduces the thoughtform as a functional analytic construct with a long, heterogeneous
genealogy in initiation, ritual, and esoteric reflection, but does not rely on metaphysical claims.
A thoughtform is defined here as a recursively sustained symbolic formation that organizes
attention, emotion, identity, interpretation, and action across people, media, institutions, and
machines. A six-stage Liminal Thoughtform Cycle explains how threshold disruption can
produce either adaptive integration or cognitive capture. The article then advances liminal
security and Cognitive Aikido as agency-centered defenses, treating mental health and well-
being as capacities for sustaining meaning, relationships, reality orientation, and action under
pressure. The objective is capacity rather than control: preserving reflective freedom, relational
coherence, and meaningful action under persistent influence.

Keywords: cognitive security, cognitive warfare, liminality, thoughtforms, influence operations,
agency, resilience

articles.title: The Accountability Gap in Sub-Sovereign ESG Finance: A Case Study of Police Administration Oversight in Chiba Prefecture, Japan
articles.authors: Takashi Miyazawa
articles.abstract: This paper examines a critical vulnerability in the methodology of sub-sovereign ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) ratings, utilizing Chiba Prefecture, Japan, as a primary case study. While global ESG frameworks increasingly evaluate local government bonds, rating agencies predominantly rely on macro-level socioeconomic indicators and overarching policy frameworks, creating a significant "measurement gap." We demonstrate how this macro-dependence obscures micro-level governance failures—specifically, the indefinite suspension of complaint processing and the systemic non-creation of official records within police administration. By applying an axiomatic approach grounded in administrative law and corporate governance principles, this study empirically documents the existence of a structural "Accountability Gap" at the operational entry point. The findings highlight the critical need for institutional investors and ESG rating agencies to discount the reliability of sub-sovereign sustainability representations when auditable management evidence is structurally absent.

articles.title: Negotiating mobility: Methodological insights from older adults' activity diaries
articles.authors: Amber DeJohn; Ainsley Bowie
articles.abstract: Older adults' mobility is a growing area of research, with multiple methods being employed to understand whether older adults can adequately access key destinations. This has resulted in increased interest in older adults' activity spaces, and a concomitant rise in methods employed to work with these individuals. While GPS-based data collection has advantages, traditional paper surveys remain in use due to their perceived low barriers to entry for participants and researchers. Relatively little is known regarding the appropriateness and validity of paper-based, self-reported activity diary data collection with older adults. Using qualitative feedback on activity diary surveys deployed in rural and urban communities and the activity diaries themselves, we argue that paper, self-reported activity diaries are viable instruments for recording older adults’ geographies. Further, qualitative feedback demonstrates how older adults confront their mobility, memories, and communities. We identify perceived mobility deficits, difficulties remembering, community visibility, and positive affect among our participants. Our findings suggest participating in activity diary surveys is a generally positive experience for older adults, but for some may engender a sense of inadequacy regardless of their activity level. We make recommendations for methodological enhancements specific to working with older adults.

articles.title: The weaponised Ocean and marine spatial planning
articles.authors: Joseph Scott Boyle; Diana Volpe
articles.abstract:
Restrictive asylum and border policies force people into dangerous maritime crossings and lead to record numbers of deaths at sea. Yet marine spatial planning (MSP), despite commitments to social benefit and expanding attention to diverse marine uses and stakeholders, has largely overlooked irregular migration and the governance regimes that shape these routes and their lethality. Applying border geographies literature to European seas, we highlight the Ocean as a weapon used to control migration and allow states to shift responsibility onto migrants.

In this Short Communication, we argue that the weaponisation of the sea through deterrence, pushbacks, neglect, and externalised border control should be recognised as an issue of marine governance. While MSP has limited scope to resolve structural drivers of displacement or border violence, it can no longer remain silent on spatially patterned forms of ‘liquid violence’. Analysing irregular migration through MSP could support more just and humanitarian Ocean governance through improved spatial understanding of migration routes, risks, and sites of death, and by aligning planning more explicitly with the protection of human life at sea. We argue that irregular maritime migration and death at sea should be understood as concerns for marine governance because they are spatially patterned, politically produced, and shaped by the allocation of visibility, safety, and responsibility at sea. As migration drivers continue to increase, acknowledging and addressing these neglected realities is an urgent task for marine policy and planning.

articles.title: Maximizing Recruitment via Respondent-driven Sampling
articles.authors: Mariel Leonard; Julian B. Axenfeld; Hannah Bethge; Julia Witton; Carina Cornesse; Sabine Zinn
articles.abstract: Respondent-driven sampling (RDS), a network-based method of sampling has become increasingly popular as a means of developing subgroup samples, particularly in web-first or web-only design (webRDS). WebRDS can reduce participant burden as well as increase the potential size and geographic scope of the sample, allowing for development of national samples with greater generalizability. However, webRDS can also introduce technical challenges as it requires all RDS processes to be mediated through internet-communication technology. In this paper, we focus on the challenges of engaging participants and reducing burden following a request to participate in webRDS. We present the results of two studies in which we tested several design features for their effects on webRDS recruitment success. We use social exchange theory as a lens through which to improve webRDS recruitment by maximizing benefits of participation and reducing burden. Based on our findings, we present recommendations for webRDS implementation.

articles.title: Digital media and social inequality : a primer in the context of Swiss digital society
articles.authors: Moritz Büchi
articles.abstract: Digital media innovations are used differently by people from different social groups and have varying consequences. Research has not found that these divides are narrowing. On the contrary, individuals who are socially better positioned appear to benefit more from digital media transformation. At the societal level, there is a need for a transparent negotiation of the values underlying the digital media infrastructure - values that can guide democratic governance.

articles.title: ‘My spiritual path is Belonging’: Belonging as a valued and sought after affective state for spiritual but not religious individuals.
articles.authors: Kathryn Diane Ford; Sotirios Kolios; Lora Adair; Matthew Michel Gervais; Aiyana Koka Willard; Michelle Ann Kline
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Objective: Spiritual but not religious (SBNR) beliefs are often characterised as hyper individualistic and lacking community. This study explores concepts of belonging and community among spiritual seekers to assess these claims. 
Methods: This study entailed 30 semi-structured interviews of SBNR individuals combined with long term ethnographic research in Glastonbury UK, a small town with a reputation as a spiritual hub. 
Results: Thematic analysis of participant interviews highlighted the importance of affective belonging to participants. Participants left social contexts where they experienced a lack of affective belonging. Participants invested time and effort into finding sources of affective belonging and in creating sources of affective belonging for others.
Conclusion: Affective belonging is important to SBNR individuals. Prior research suggesting that spiritual but not religious do not value belonging is due primarily to miss-measurement and a lack of conceptual clarity. 
Key words: Spiritual but not Religious, Belonging, Community, Glastonbury, Belief, Qualitative, Interviews

articles.title: Geometry Proposes, Judgement Disposes: Accurate Online Proposal Clustering for Digital Deliberation
articles.authors: Tal Yaron; Fany Yuval
articles.abstract: Digital deliberation requires accurate clustering of proposals: equivalent contributions should be joined, while related interventions and opposing positions remain distinct. We study an online method implemented in Freedi that uses embeddings to retrieve candidates and focused language-model judgements to authorize synthesis, with separate themes, retained sources, and maintenance. We explain its retrieval-judgement interface and seven-stage selection process and compare it with the two main alternatives, cosine rules and LLM-only grouping. On 875 counterfactual preference triplets, a component study achieves 95.0%-96.5% accept-and-reject accuracy with original-text judging, compared with 0% for the tested cosine decision rule. On a controlled English corpus, Freedi and LLM-only baselines recover all 50 intended pairs in three arrival orders. A new 240-call probe on one authentic English deliberation compares full-list judgement with judgement over 15 retrieved proposals. Median per-decision cost reductions grow from 2.55-fold at 100 proposals to 4.29-fold at 200 and 9.38-fold at 500, under common base token prices. At 500 proposals, agreement with provisional model-authored labels is 25/40 for the restricted list and 31/40 for the full list. Retrieved targets remain available, but the restricted judge declines more merges. These refusals may preserve substantive distinctions in scope or intervention; whether they improve semantic precision or constitute missed matches requires human adjudication. A separate replay of 114 Hebrew statements shows improved automated merge precision and text fidelity after combined repairs. The evidence supports semantic judgement over the tested cosine rules and a growing cost advantage for candidate reduction at the measured scales. Equal accuracy and lower total cost for the complete Freedi pipeline remain to be established.

articles.title: Pre-modern checks and balances: an analysis of hunter-gatherer cultures
articles.authors: Honorata Mazepus; Natália Kubalová; Alexander Mangun; Elena Cecconi
articles.abstract: Although support for democratic values remains high across the world, political scientists report the erosion of institutional checks and balances. Why do citizens allow dismantling of democratic institutions? Does it mean that contemporary institutions for constraining authorities do not resonate with our human minds? In this paper we take the first steps to identify the pre-modern "original" mechanisms to constrain and empower authorities by investigating hunter-gatherer communities. Through the analysis of ethnographic records in the eHRAF World Cultures database, we examine (1) under what conditions hunter-gatherers empowered and constrained their leaders and (2) what mechanisms they used to prevent the abuse of power. In this pilot study, we analysed 1,106 paragraphs describing six cultures from different regions of the world and with different socio-political organization. Our analyses point to a set of possible political intuitions triggered by the challenges faced by a subset of hunter-gatherer communities. Preliminary findings show aversion towards domination, vigilance and punishment of rule violations, preference for competence-based leadership and majority decision-making. Our results suggest that democratic backsliding might not be due to the general incompatibility of checks and balances with the human intuitions about politics, but rather that the combination of the design of our institutions and the specific circumstances might enable democratic erosion.

articles.title: One Policy, Many Publics: Central Bank Communication and the National Politics of Trust
articles.authors: Björn Bremer; Lucio Baccaro
articles.abstract: Central bank decisions have become politically contested. In response, central banks communicate more with the public, since their effectiveness rests on public trust. Yet whether they reach ordinary citizens is largely unknown. We exploit the European Central Bank’s unexpected announcement of the Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme (PEPP) during the fieldwork of a March 2020 survey in Germany and Italy. Our results show that the same decisive intervention was rewarded only where it aligned with the perceived national interest: in Italy, trust in the ECB rose, strongest among news-followers and the left; in Germany, trust in the ECB did not move at all, even as trust in national institutions surged. Preferences for central bank goal independence moved in neither country. Citizens thus notice exceptional monetary policy decisions, but their responses are mediated by national interests and discourses, with asymmetric consequences for a central bank that makes one policy for many publics.

articles.title: When Aging No Longer Means Turning Right: Evidence from Swiss Panel Data
articles.authors: Lena Ajdacic; Matthias Enggist; Reto Mitteregger
articles.abstract:
By adopting a generational lens, research has increasingly documented political and electoral
transformations in Western Europe. In parallel, many researchers have pointed to the
crucial relevance of the formative years to understand attitudinal development.
However, these approaches often dismiss that generations’ formative years can differ,
with newer generations marrying later, having fewer children, and completing education
later in life. Using data from the Swiss Household Panel (1999-2022), we analyze
whether different generations in Switzerland show diverging age effects regarding
political ideology. Find-ings from an interaction analysis of age and cohort show that
while previous generations consistently tended to become more right-wing as they aged,
members of Generations Y and Z remain largely stable in their ideological orientation
over the life course. We find that this pattern is not explained by changes in
demographic and socio-economic compo-sition between cohorts. The results of this study
not only have important implications for future studies analyzing age-period-cohort
effects, but also enhance our understanding of opinion formation in transforming postindustrial
societies.

articles.title: From Networks to Mission Platforms: A Graded Architecture for Interdisciplinary Research at Institutional Scale
articles.authors: Jesus Marco de Lucas; Victoria Moreno-Arribas
articles.abstract:
Large multidisciplinary research organisations face a well-documented tension: their breadth is
precisely what makes them suited to complex societal challenges, yet their disciplinary structure
(centres, areas, evaluation panels) makes interdisciplinary work costly to initiate and hard to sustain.
This paper presents a longitudinal institutional case study of the approach adopted by the Spanish
National Research Council (CSIC) — Spain’s largest public research organisation, with more than
1,500 research groups in around 120 institutes — to address that tension without restructuring the
institution. From 2018 onward CSIC developed a graded set of three collaboration instruments:
Conexiones (light, bottom-up thematic networks), Interdisciplinary Thematic Platforms (PTI: mission-
oriented, three-year, challenge-driven platforms with an ESFRI-derived design questionnaire) and
Extended Platforms (PTI+: large-scale platforms with a four-line work structure, a consortium-
agreement style governance and centralised financial management, created to absorb investments
above C10M). The design principles of each instrument, the formal texts that implemented them and
the governance rules are presented (dual coordination across centres, assembly/executive-committee
model, two-thirds quorum, individual veto, VICYT ratification, Team Science and Open Science
recommendations). Publicly available documentary evidence on outcomes up to 31 August 2026
is then compiled for the best-documented platforms and networks, including the PTI Salud Global
response to COVID-19, the QTEP quantum ecosystem, SusPlast pilot plants, the IPCC Interactive Atlas
delivered under PTI Clima, the Conexiones cohorts created in 2023 and 2025, and the 2026 migration
of the Teledetect remote-sensing platform into the EarthWatchHub Conexión. The documentary record
supports four observations: (i) a pre-existing platform template enabled unusually rapid institutional
mobilisation during COVID-19; (ii) the platform architecture and its core governance principles were
adapted to an increase of roughly two orders of magnitude in financial scale; (iii) a graded portfolio
allowed organisational migration between instruments instead of simple termination; and (iv) different
instruments generated documented joint activities and outputs. The instruments were subsequently
formalised, not discontinued, by the administration that succeeded the one that created them. A set
of transferable design propositions is derived from the case, and the limitations of a documentary
analysis without a counterfactual are discussed. The contribution is a longitudinal institutional case
showing how a large disciplinary research organisation can superimpose a graded set of transverse
collaboration structures on its existing organisational backbone without dismantling it.

articles.title: Do Voters Blame the Opposition for Losing in Electoral Autocracies? Evidence from Turkey
articles.authors: Jonas Draege; Philipp Lutscher
articles.abstract: How do voters in autocracies evaluate opposition performance after defeat? We study this question with an exploratory online survey of 1054 opposition voters six months after Turkey's 2023 presidential and parliamentary elections. Although the opposition operated under structural disadvantages typical of electoral autocracies, nearly two-thirds of opposition voters blamed the opposition for the loss. Open-ended responses reveal three sources of dissatisfaction: criticism of the presidential candidate, frustration with intra-coalition conflict, and discomfort with the ideological breadth of the alliance. While these concerns often reflected genuine weaknesses in the opposition campaign, several were also intertwined with constraints imposed by the authoritarian context. To capture this tension, we introduce the concept of the authoritarian double bind: opposition parties are constrained by the regime in ways that produce the very weaknesses for which voters hold them accountable. Our findings show how electoral autocracies can simultaneously constrain opposition performance while voters continue to hold the opposition accountable for electoral failure.

articles.title: Framing the Border as a National Security Threat: Fox News Immigration Coverage in the 2016 and 2024 Election Cycles
articles.authors: Jenny Xu
articles.abstract: While previous scholarship has established the existence of U.S. right-wing ideological media framing and its evolution over time, there is limited research exploring how influential outlets like Fox News have framed immigration across two critical election cycles: 2016 and 2024. These years represent key moments in recent American history, extreme-right-wing media narratives, and how that shapes public perception of emotionally charged topics, such as that of “illegal immigration” in the United States. This research paper explores the question: How has Fox News framed the U.S.–Mexico border and immigration policy during election cycles, particularly in 2016 and 2024? It argues that Fox News strategically frames immigration as a national security threat during the 2016 and 2024 election cycles. I conduct a content analysis of the language, guests, and visuals used on Fox News programming, such as Hannity, to highlight how Fox News deliberately intensified its framing of the U.S.–Mexico border as a national security threat to influence public perception and invoke fear. This paper contributes to the fields of media studies and political communication by providing a multi-year analysis of threat-based storytelling that Fox News uses to shape public opinion. It deepens our understanding of the interplay between media bias, national security threats, and commercial incentives.

articles.title: Demographic Decline and Economic Challenges in East Asia: A Comparative Analysis of the Republic of Korea, Japan, and China
articles.authors: Piyush Shrestha
articles.abstract: Although the Republic of Korea, Japan, and China are experiencing similarly rapid fertility decline and population aging, the socioeconomic consequences of these changes differ considerably across the three countries. Population decline does not operate through a single mechanism; rather, its effects are shaped by the structural conditions of households, labor markets, and local economies. Unlike Korea, where demographic anxiety is heavily concentrated in the overheated metropolitan housing market, Japan absorbs its aging burden primarily through a bifurcated labor system. China complicates this regional narrative further. Despite a shrinking national population, the slowing domestic economy is paradoxically struggling to absorb a record influx of university graduates. Across the three countries, unpaid care work remains unevenly distributed between women and men, adding to the pressures surrounding employment, marriage, and family formation.
