These differences imply that demographic policy cannot rely on a uniform set of incentives. Therefore, policy interventions are more likely to be effective when they respond to the particular institutional and socioeconomic constraints operating within each country.

articles.title: Ecological Sensemaking as a Recursive Process of Indigenous Climate Adaptation: Evidence from the Santal Community of Bangladesh
articles.authors: Sourav Paul Chowdhury; Syed M. Ali Reza; M. Nasim Reza; Dhanno Saha; Solaiman Chowdhury
articles.abstract: Climate adaptation research has focused more on adaptive capacity, technological innovation, and resilience, and less on the interpretive processes that lie before adaptive action. In this study, ecological sensemaking is investigated as a factor influencing agricultural decision-making among the Santal indigenous community in Barind region, which is prone to drought in Bangladesh. The research employed an interpretivist paradigm using thematic analysis of 25 semi-structured interviews. The findings indicate that adaptation starts with the ongoing process of interpreting ecological cues in a way that is negotiated through indigenous ecological knowledge, lived experience, scientific information, and social interaction. Four interrelated themes account for the process of the construction of ecological meanings, their translation to agricultural and livelihood practices, and how they are constrained by structural conditions. The study goes beyond organizational contexts to describe and explain ecological sensemaking, reconceptualizing indigenous ecological knowledge as a process of environmental meaning-making, and proposes a process-based conceptual model for climate adaptation in the face of ecological uncertainty. The study extends Weick's Sensemaking Theory by conceptualizing ecological sensemaking as a recursive, relational, and structurally mediated process operating within Indigenous socio-ecological systems, thereby offering a theoretically grounded understanding of climate adaptation beyond organizational settings.

articles.title: Too Much Detail Kills the Vibe: Quantifying Lyrical Realism and Pop Music Virality
articles.authors: Muhammad Sukri Bin Ramli
articles.abstract: Pop music songwriters frequently deploy vivid real-world anchors, such as specific vehicle models and city names, to establish narrative realism. However, whether hyper-specific realism systematically drives commercial virality remains an unexamined empirical question. In this paper, we introduce an open-science computational framework that quantifies lyrical realism across 27 tracks from EDM-pop duo The Chainsmokers (2014-2024). By combining Brysbaert psycholinguistic concreteness norms (ILCA), named entity density, VADER sentiment analysis, and sentence embeddings with log-transformed YouTube view counts, we evaluate the structural drivers of pop virality. Statistical analysis reveals a negative rank correlation (Spearman r = -0.632, p < 0.001, 95% Confidence Interval [-0.814, -0.381]) and quadratic regression confirms a concave curvilinear relationship (quadratic beta = -2.18, p = 0.004), providing preliminary evidence consistent with a possible Inverted-U pattern. An estimated candidate optimal concreteness range (ILCA between 2.75 and 2.90) characterizes high-performing crossover tracks, whereas hyper-concreteness (ILCA greater than 3.20) marks a substantial reduction in streaming reach by over-saturating narrative details and restricting listener self-projection. Exploratory TreeSHAP attributions indicate that physical anchors must be balanced with chorus repetition and nostalgic sentiment to optimize streaming reach. All code, figure files, and datasets are open-sourced for computational reproducibility.

articles.title: Does belief in supernatural punishment increase prosociality? Evidence from economic games in two religiously pluralistic communities of southern Benin
articles.authors: Augusto Dalla Ragione; Cody T. Ross; Marina Elodie Sedjro Djekinnou; Iranlowo Abakpin Elodie F Lawin; As’Ad Olawale Ichola Assani; Tossou Jeandro Simplice Kakpo; Daniel Major-Smith; Benjamin Grant Purzycki
articles.abstract: The role and durability of religious institutions in human societies has long been the subject of discussion among social scientists. A prominent view in anthropology considers religions-and especially moralistic religions-as institutions that enhance within-group cooperative proclivities and minimize norm violations, by inducing belief in the threat of supernatural punishment and monitoring. This may be particularly important in sustaining cooperation in larger groups, where mechanisms based on kinship, reciprocity, and reputation bookkeeping are less likely to be effective. The empirical literature is mixed, with some standardized cross-cultural studies providing support for claims of a relationship between moralistic punishment/monitoring beliefs and prosociality. For this study, we collected a suite of survey data on sociodemographics and religiosity, and ran economic experiments in two communities in southern Benin, West Africa. The communities are Vodun-majority, with an appreciable presence of Christians. This local religious diversity within the same ecological setting allows us to: (1) study the degree of syncretism between the two traditions, (2) evaluate whether Vodun and Christian believers attribute different levels of moralistic concerns to their respective deities, and (3) address the impact of belief in supernatural punishment on prosociality, as well as test for  differences in effects between adherents of the two traditions. Our analyses reveal some statistically reliable associations between measures of religious cognition and experimental behavior, with increased perception of moralistic supernatural punishment being predictive of higher levels of prosociality. Our results, however, are sensitive to how religious cognition is measured, the type of prosocial behavior considered, and the specific religious community under study. We discuss our results within the framework of leading hypotheses on the nexus between religion and prosociality.

articles.title: Housing Populism Under Financialized Capitalism
articles.authors: Rafaela Dancygier; Vincent Heddesheimer; Andreas Wiedemann
articles.abstract: This paper examines the rise of housing populism: narratives casting financial investors as predatory and policies demanding investor bans. We argue that housing populism is politically appealing less because it reflects economic realities than because it resonates with public moral commitments: distrust of financialized capitalism and support for housing as a collective entitlement. Drawing on two decades of property-level transaction data, we demonstrate that institutional investors account for a very small share of housing transactions and have limited effects on housing costs. Original surveys reveal, however, that voters overestimate investor activity, believe that investors undermine the right to housing, and demand that the government safeguards access. Experimental evidence shows that politicians advocating investor bans via rights-based or anti-predatory frames substantially outperform those prioritizing home-building through pragmatic or market-oriented appeals. Housing populism channels social-rights claims into symbolic confrontations between ``the people'' and financial elites, often displacing more effective policy responses.

articles.title: Posting, Liking, and Messaging: The Correspondence Between Self-Reported and Actual Activities on Instagram and the Role of Question Framing
articles.authors: Frieder Rodewald; Florian Keusch; Daria Szafran; Ruben L. Bach
articles.abstract: Research comparing self-reported and actual online behavior has focused primarily on general usage, such as how often individuals visit a platform or how much time they spend on it, and less on on-platform activities such as posting, commenting, or liking. We use respondents' actual behavior on Instagram, obtained through data donation, to examine how self-reports correspond to actual behavior, both for general usage frequency and for six on-platform activities. We test whether the direction of deviations between the two measures varies systematically with how often individuals actually use Instagram and how frequently they engage in each activity. We also test whether question framing affects correspondence for activities in a 2×2 survey experiment that varies the reference period (last seven days vs. typical week) and the response scale (numeric vs. vague quantifier labels). In a pre-registered study based on a probability-based online panel in Germany (n = 428 data donors), we find that self-reports of general usage frequency fall below actual usage for most respondents, and most so among frequent users. For on-platform activities, self-reports match actual behavior more often than they deviate from it, and the direction of deviations varies across activities. Higher actual engagement predicts underreporting for nearly all activities, whereas the association between lower engagement and overreporting is less stable. Contrary to expectations, the reference period does not improve correspondence for any activity, and numeric quantifier labels yield closer correspondence than vague quantifier labels for several activities. We discuss what these patterns imply for what self-reports and digital traces measure, and derive practical guidance for survey design in digital media research.

articles.title: For Whom Neighborhoods Matter in Early Childhood: Heterogeneous Effects on Achievement
articles.authors: Nicolai T. Borgen; Henrik Daae Zachrisson; Rosa Cheesman; Torkild Hovde Lyngstad; Eivind Ystrom
articles.abstract: The role of neighborhoods in shaping child and adolescent development is well-documented in empirical research. However, the extent to which neighborhood conditions differentially affect individuals based on their background and individual characteristics remains less explored, particularly during the first decade of life. This paper investigates the heterogeneous effects of neighborhood socioeconomic composition on academic achievement in middle childhood by combining Norwegian administrative data with genetic data from the Norwegian Mother, Father, and Child Cohort Study (MoBa). Employing the Neighborhood Choice Model to address selection bias, we find that exposure to neighborhood disadvantage during a child's first ten years impacts 5th-grade standardized test scores. Furthermore, we find that the impact of neighborhoods varies considerably by socioeconomic background, gender, and children’s load for genetic variants correlated with educational attainment, estimated using within-family genetic variation. Notably, boys, children with a lower polygenic index for educational attainment, and those from families with lower incomes and parental education levels face the strongest neighborhood effects. Conversely, children with a higher polygenic index for education are unaffected by neighborhood disadvantage, as are children with affluent parents. These findings highlight the importance of studying heterogeneous neighborhood effects.

articles.title: What Instagram Records and What Users Report: A Data Donation Study Comparing Digital Traces with Self-Reported Behavior
articles.authors: Frieder Rodewald; Florian Keusch; Daria Szafran; Ruben L. Bach
articles.abstract: Understanding how individuals use social media is central to research on its effects, yet most studies rely on self-reports. It remains unclear which behaviors platforms record at all, how closely self-reports correspond to those records, and how question design affects that correspondence. In a data donation study with a German probability-based online panel (N = 531 Instagram users, of whom 121 donated their data), we identified 93 digital traces available in Instagram's data download packages and extracted 49, spanning consumption, engagement, creation, and account management. Prevalence follows a steep gradient: consumption traces such as viewing are near-universal, engagement traces such as liking appear for a majority, creation traces such as posting appear for only a minority, and many specialized features are absent altogether, so several behaviors of potential interest can be studied only within the subgroup performing them. Self-reports correspond reasonably to actual behavior for deliberate, frequent behaviors (e.g., creating stories, liking posts), but poorly for passive consumption and rare behaviors. Experimentally varying the reference period and response format, we find significantly higher correlations under a typical-week framing for one behavior and no significant differences between response formats. We discuss when self-reports may suffice and when donated data is needed.

articles.title: Understanding the connection between parental and filial aspirations - Do family relationships matter?
articles.authors: Kerstin Schörner; Monja Schmitt; Felix Bittmann
articles.abstract: Educational aspirations are a key driver of educational inequalities. This article explores how such aspirations are transmitted within families, drawing on psychological research and extending the Wisconsin Model. Challenging its assumption of a universal parental influence on children’s aspirations, we build on Coleman’s notion of an interplay between human and social capital. We argue that high parental aspirations shape children’s aspirations only when there is close intrafamily exchange, which builds the channel to transmit parental aspirations to children. Using data from the National Educational Panel Study, we distinguish between realistic and idealistic aspirations from 6,053 children and their parents and structural and process related aspects of intrafamily social capital. A series of linear probability models find assumed interaction effects only for realistic aspirations and process-related aspects of intrafamily social capital. Consequently, high parental aspirations are specifically transmitted to children when there is strong and close interaction within the family and aspirations are understood as expectations.

articles.title: The Dark Side of Legitimation. Experimental Evidence on the Effectiveness of Discursive Strategies Used by Cyber Criminals
articles.authors: Kristina Sabrina Weißmüller; Tijs van den Broek; Alina Kaufmann; Steven James Watson
articles.abstract: Online, criminal organizations regularly use discursive legitimation strategies to influence public opinion about their criminal activities to justify their acts and minimize persecution. Yet, little is known about what types of strategies are effective in the case of criminal organizations. This study addresses this gap by identifying and quantifying how distinct discursive strategies impact citizens’ legitimacy judgment, their attribution of blame for societal harm associated with criminal activity and punitive intent. Using a discrete choice experiment conducted with representative citizen samples in Germany (n=301, Obs.=1,505) and the United Kingdom (n=350, Obs.=1,750), the study shows that distinct strategies can significantly impact citizens’ judgment about the legitimacy of criminal activity, their attribution of responsibility, accountability, and punitive intent. Cognitive and moral legitimation strategies – such as discrediting victims and legitimate institutions, but also signaling transparency and moralizing criminal action – are most effective. Social media amplifies, and higher societal harm reduces the influence of legitimation strategies. These novel insights advance the discourse on organizational legitimacy in the post-factual age of digital communication as well as scholarship on accountability and public opinion on criminal activity, helping practitioners and policy makers understand and counteract legitimation efforts by criminal organizations.

articles.title: Decentralization, Ethnic Fractionalization, and Public Services:  Evidence from Kenyan Healthcare
articles.authors: Camille Hémet; Liam Wren-Lewis; Jessica Mahoney
articles.abstract: This paper examines the impact of ethnic fractionalization on public service use by exploiting a major constitutional reform in Kenya.  Following an important period of inter-ethnic conflict, responsibility for local health services was decentralized to 47 newly created county governments.  Using an event-study design, we find that use of public clinics for births increased significantly after the reform, but only in counties that were relatively ethnically homogeneous.  We also find a significant increase in the correlation between county ethnic fractionalization and a range of other measures of public health service use.  Services in these counties are also less likely to require payments after decentralization.  Using within-county variation to investigate mechanisms, we find healthcare use increases were concentrated among areas and individuals  of the same ethnicity as members of the new county government executives.  Overall, the results suggest that more ethnically homogeneous sub-national jurisdictions can rapidly increase public service use.

articles.title: Sequential Structure Without a Linguistic Diagnosis: A Falsification-Oriented Analysis of the Indus Script
articles.authors: Joy Bose
articles.abstract: The Indus Valley script remains undeciphered. Under ordinary cross-validated scoring, real Indus sign sequences show a positive trigram-over-bigram predictive gain (the two preceding signs predict the next sign better than one preceding sign alone), replicating closely across two independently extracted digitizations of the same underlying corpus tradition, including the M77 corpus corresponding to the concordance behind the most cited statistical studies of the script (+0.143 and +0.158 bits), and clearing 200-trial null distributions entirely. However, both corpora contain substantial exact-sequence repetition (23 to 33 percent of sequences). When cross-validation folds are constructed so duplicate sequences cannot appear in both training and their own held-out evaluation, the gain reverses sign for both corpora (-0.088, -0.083); when duplicates are instead collapsed to unique sequence types, it weakens to near zero (-0.023, -0.010). A control experiment, grouping sequences of the same size distribution but without duplicate identity, stays strongly positive, ruling out the alternative explanation that this reversal simply reflects smaller effective training sets rather than duplicate identity specifically. This is not a data-handling error, since the repetition is a genuine corpus property, but it means the ordinary-CV result should not be read as established evidence of sequential structure that generalizes to novel sequences, and we treat resolving this as the paper's central open problem. Independently of that question, our most specific test among the mechanisms we examined shows the ordinary-CV gain is not uniquely diagnostic of the particular linguistic generative mechanism we tested, including after rebuilding that generator and a non-linguistic alternative to match the real corpus's own vocabulary and length statistics; neither reproduces the real magnitude in matched or unmatched form. A sample-size curve on two calibration languages shows this estimator rarely returns a positive result below roughly 3,000 sequences for either, evidence against the ordinary-CV result being generic small-sample behavior. We also find evidence against inscriptions being deliberately constructed as globally unique identifiers, though not against more elaborate identifier schemes. The framework, derived corpora where licensing permits, and all experiments are released openly.

articles.title: Even More Unequal Childhoods: 45 Years of Widening Income Gaps in Parental Investments in the United States
articles.authors: Orestes P Hastings
articles.abstract: Parents can convert economic resources into advantages and opportunities for their children through spending on goods, services, and experiences. Using data from the 1980–2024 Consumer Expenditure Survey, this study provides the most comprehensive account to date of income-group trends in parental financial investments in childcare, education, and extracurricular activities. Income gaps widened throughout these 45 years. Per-child spending in the top decile nearly quadrupled in real terms, while bottom-quartile spending was slightly lower in 2024 than in 1980. Thus, the top decile spent roughly three times as much per child as the bottom quartile in the early 1980s but more than thirteen times as much by 2024. This widening spans all three categories, is also reflected in the share of households’ total budgets directed toward spending on children, and is driven more by how much households spend than by whether they spend at all. These findings document a sustained widening of income gaps in parental financial investments in the United States, pointing to these expenditures as an increasingly important dimension of unequal childhoods.

articles.title: When Do Autocratizing Incumbents Lose Elections?
articles.authors: Erin Hern; Marc S. Jacob
articles.abstract: When do electorates remove incumbents who undermine democracy? Existing research offers accounts of why electorates tolerate autocratizing leaders, but has paid less attention to cases when they hold them accountable. We develop a framework of electoral accountability under autocratization to evaluate when attacks on democracy trigger electoral backlash, considering the scope of autocratization (i.e., the breadth of institutional erosion) and its overtness (i.e., whether autocratizing acts are carried out openly through coercion rather than through subtle institutional change), alongside preexisting institutional strength, economic performance, and political culture. Drawing on an original dataset of 105 elections since 1995 in which autocratizing incumbents sought re-election, hand-coded measures of autocratization scope and overtness in recent electoral contests, experimental evidence, and comparative analyses of Poland and Zambia, we find that overtness, but not scope, is systematically linked to incumbent defeat. Our findings have implications for the conditions under which citizens can disrupt episodes of autocratization through electoral channels.

articles_hidden.title: Bucks for Bumps: How Paid Parental Leave Pays Off for Firms
articles_hidden.authors: Hillary Cookler
articles_hidden.abstract: Firms use benefits such as paid parental leave (PPL) to attract and retain employees. In the U.S., which lacks broad public PPL benefits, firms increasingly provide this benefit. Systematic evidence of its benefits remains limited, due in part to the absence of comprehensive data on firm policies. Using a novel, hand-collected database of firm policy changes, this paper estimates the causal effect of PPL expansion on employee retention using a differences-in-differences approach. PPL expansions reduce departure rates by 3.1%, an effect equivalent to a permanent wage increase of 1.8%. Retention gains for women are concentrated among the lowest paid and those in the most junior roles, while retention gains for men are broad-based. At the firm level, retention gains concentrate in the interior of the internal labor market flexibility distribution and among firms with moderate firm-specific human capital, and they are robust to concurrent benefit changes and to firm revenue trajectories. Public PPL programs, by contrast, show no comparable retention effect, consistent with the non-portability of firm-provided benefits. Combining fertility estimates from the American Community Survey (ACS) with worker and firm data, the paper calculates the expected costs of PPL provision and compares them to retention gains: at realistic utilization rates, PPL expansions generate positive net returns to firms.

articles_hidden.title: A Rough Revised Estimate of Exclusive Breastfeeding at 6 Months in England Based on the 2024 Infant Feeding Survey
articles_hidden.authors: Emily H Emmott
articles_hidden.abstract: The 2024 Infant Feeding Survey likely overestimates exclusive breastfeeding prevalence at 6 months in England. Roughly correcting for probable selection and attrition bias, true prevalence is more plausibly in the region of 4–17%, with an upper bound estimate of 21.4%. More precise estimates would require individual level data, which would allow formal modelling and direct estimation of differential attrition by feeding status.

articles_hidden.title: The Growing Transatlantic Sanctions Divide
articles_hidden.authors: Anton Peez
articles_hidden.abstract: Multilateral cooperation on sanctions is a key determinant of their success, yet transatlantic collaboration on sanctions is steeply declining. This transatlantic sanctions divide is a symptom of increasingly divergent US and EU foreign policies. Sanctions are likewise best terminated multilaterally to effectively wield them as leverage. Here too, trustful US-EU collaboration is increasingly difficult to imagine. Nonetheless, strong public support for sanctioning Russia in both the EU and US offers a basis for continuing forceful Western sanctions as Russia escalates its war of aggression against Ukraine.

articles_hidden.title: Generational Imprinting: How Political Events Shape Cohorts
articles_hidden.authors: Turgut Keskintürk
articles_hidden.abstract: Contemporary narratives of generational politics propose that formative experiences produce shared political opinions across an age cohort. In this article, I advance a theory of cohortization to challenge that view, arguing that large-scale political events produce differentiation within cohorts as much as differentiation between them. I investigate the implications of this framework through the killing of George Floyd and the subsequent Black Lives Matter protests in 2020, analyzing attitudes toward law enforcement among non-Hispanic White Americans from 2016 to 2024. Using survey data from Cooperative Congressional Election Study, American National Election Study, and the Nationscape, I show that younger and older cohorts diverged after the event, but this differentiation was driven exclusively by young Democrats and Independents. The end result was not a unified generation, but one internally divided along party lines. This finding qualifies theories of generational politics, emphasizing that formative experiences may intensify existing political divisions within cohorts.

articles_hidden.title: Constructing Methodologically Robust Subnational Estimates from Survey Microdata: A Methods Review
articles_hidden.authors: Kailas Venkitasubramanian
articles_hidden.abstract:
Constructing estimates for a custom, county-defined region from survey microdata is constrained by
the geography at which respondents are identified. In the American Community Survey (ACS) Public
Use Microdata Sample (PUMS), that geography is the Public Use Microdata Area (PUMA), which
does not nest into counties and is periodically redrawn. This review surveys the state of the art in
producing methodologically robust subnational estimates under these constraints, organized into four
method families — crosswalk and allocation-factor methods, consistent-geography harmonization, areal
interpolation and dasymetric and structure-preserving methods, and model-based small-area estimation.
Each family is assessed against a reference baseline: a population-weighted allocation-factor pipeline
with Successive Difference Replication variance estimation. The review pays particular attention to the
within-zone compositional homogeneity assumption that limits direct reweighting, to the harmonization
of geographies across boundary revisions, and to the rigor of uncertainty quantification. It restricts
attention to methods implementable with publicly available data. It serves both as a standalone reference
and as the methodological foundation for a companion analysis.

articles_hidden.title: A Stacked Deck: Ambition, Supply, Demand, and Women’s Access to Political Power
articles_hidden.authors: Mirya Holman; Lakshmi Iyer; Christina Wolbrecht
articles_hidden.abstract: Why do women remain underrepresented in positions of political power? A central challenge to answering this question is the difficulty in disentangling possible explanations, including women’s lack of interest or ambition, differences in women’s preparedness for political office, and discrimination against women by selectors. In this paper, we are uniquely able to investigate all three kinds of explanations simultaneously. Our unique dataset of applicants to appointed boards at the local level in the United States contains detailed professional, civic, and political information about the applicants, as well as about the boards to which they apply and the decisions of the appointers. We find that women are indeed less likely to apply for political positions, particularly powerful positions. The men and women who do apply are equally qualified. Despite these qualifications, women are less likely to be appointed to boards with more authority and power.

articles_hidden.title: Seizing the Agenda: Polarization and Legislative Autonomy in Brazilian Presidentialism
articles_hidden.authors: Jamil Civitarese; Fabiano Guilherme Mendes Santos
articles_hidden.abstract: Brazilian coalitional presidentialism has long been read as a system in which the executive sets the agenda and the legislature holds a veto. We argue that, since the mid-2010s, the Congress has been building agenda-setting power. We account for the shift with a formal spatial framework in which a legislature weighs the cost of acquiring agenda power against the costs caused by the executive it expects to face. Two forces drive the investment: the rightward movement of a median legislator dissatisfied with the status quo and the recent polarization of the Executive, a partner that became too radical and costly to legislate with. Reading the record from Lula's first governments through Lula III, we show how the realignment of agenda power came to constrain the president who now has to both manage the coalition and to accommodate increasing policy demands from the legislature.

articles_hidden.title: Economic Growth and Working-Class Representation: Evidence from Brazil
articles_hidden.authors: Jamil Civitarese
articles_hidden.abstract: Economic growth may lead to more resources for the working class to solve collective action problems and demand political representation, but not all instances of economic growth do unequivocally reduce economic inequality. When productivity gains accrue disproportionately to economic elites and political parties lack durable ties to labor, it may instead deepen class-based political exclusion. I test this argument using a novel panel that identifies the occupational background of every city council candidate in Brazil from 2004 to 2020, a period of economic growth led by agribusiness productivity increases. Within municipalities, increases in GDP are associated with a smaller share of campaign funding going to working-class candidates and a lower share of elected councilors from working-class backgrounds. Leveraging individual-level data on career trajectories of incumbents, I confirm these results. Additionally, I study the scope conditions for my theory, showing that non-leftist parties and rural areas drive my results. A qualitative comparison design reveals that discretionary choices by party leaders serve as a channel through which unequal growth can reinforce exclusion in political representation.

articles_hidden.title: Are geographical and socioeconomic contexts exchangeable? On simple means versus random effects in the study of health inequalities
articles_hidden.authors: Juan Merlo; Kani Khalaf
articles_hidden.abstract: Multilevel random-effects (RE) models are standard in social and geographical epidemiology. They rest on the assumption of exchangeability, which means that, before seeing the data, we have no reason to distinguish one group from another: group means become draws from one common distribution. RE models were developed for repeated measurements within individuals where a shared physiology underwrites the assumption, and partial pooling improves prediction. A silent transfer later applied the same machinery to schools, hospitals, neighbourhoods and, recently, to intersectional strata. There exchangeability fails twice: individuals are not repeated measurements of their group, and groups are social positions produced by directional forces such as racism, not draws from a common distribution. We review strict, conditional and tolerant readings of exchangeability and show that they agree: social and intersectional categories are not exchangeable, as this would paradoxically require the absence of the unjustified inequalities which are the very object of study. In many intersectional analyses, shrinkage erases the small and deviating strata, where inequality lives. Modelling injustice as dispersion around a mean domesticates rather than denounces it. For describing realised health inequalities we recommend Simple-Means MAIHDA (S-MAIHDA). Here, each stratum is estimated from its own individuals, and uncertainty is reported openly rather than smoothed. RE models keep their legitimate uses, such as prediction, cluster-randomised trials and the propensity models of causal S-MAIHDA. Exchangeability is not a property of the software. It is a claim about the world, to be justified in every application.

articles_hidden.title: Six-Year Trends in LGBTQ+ Youth Mental Health in the United States
articles_hidden.authors: Keith Robert Head
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of trends in LGBTQ+ youth mental health from 2019 through 2024, drawing on data from The Trevor Project’s annual national surveys. We examine five consistently measured indicators across six years of survey data including: suicidal ideation and attempts, discrimination due to SOGI (sexual orientation and gender identity), physical threats and harm exposure, and conversion therapy exposure and threats. Suicidal thoughts among LGBTQ+ youth rose to a significant peak before easing, while actual attempts showed a steady decline, especially among adolescents, yet younger teens remained disproportionately vulnerable throughout. Over the same period, discrimination remained persistently widespread, while reports of physical violence swung sharply but ended higher than at the outset, and exposure to conversion therapy spiked briefly during the pandemic era before settling back to its earlier yet still troubling level, highlighting the significant risks young LGBTQ+ youth and young adults face. The findings highlight continuing disparities, alongside small improvements in some areas. In conclusion, we summarize key insights and recommend actions to bolster mental health support, reduce stigma and victimization, and expand affirming resources for LGBTQ+ youth.

articles_hidden.title: Start-up certification and prices: Evidence from markups and a statutory expiry in Italy
articles_hidden.authors: Angelo Leogrande; Mauro Di Molfetta; Valeria Nortarnicola; Maria Giovanna Trotta; Antonio Volpe Plantamura
articles_hidden.abstract: Italy grants registered innovative start-ups fee exemptions, investor tax relief and guaranteed credit, and removes that status sixty months after incorporation. This paper asks whether certification changes firms’ markups. Markups are estimated from a translog production function on 76,466 firm-years of certified start-ups, certified innovative SMEs and ordinary SMEs over 2015–2024. Certified firms price about 12 per cent below ordinary SMEs, but within firms the gap shrinks to 2 per cent and vanishes once persistence is modelled: registration selects firms rather than changing their pricing. Exploiting the statutory expiry, and a 2020 extension that shifted it by one year for adjacent cohorts, the loss of status leaves markups unchanged on average (2SLS −0.005, first-stage F = 750). An unsupervised partition shows this null combines falls of five to six per cent in capital- and materials-intensive firms with none elsewhere; regression learners and double machine learning confirm the central estimates.

articles_hidden.title: The Human Cost of Port-Centric Development in Dar es Salaam: Displacement, Congestion and Development Without Distribution
articles_hidden.authors: Rutashubanyuma Nestory
articles_hidden.abstract: Dar es Salaam's transformation into a major regional logistics hub illustrates both the developmental promise and distributive risks of infrastructure-led growth. Modernisation of the port, expansion of inland container depots (ICDs), and investment in rail and road connectivity are essential to Tanzania's trade ambitions. Yet infrastructure expansion can generate a second problem when the costs of urban transformation are concentrated on communities living in strategically valuable locations. This article examines the relationship between port-centric development, displacement, compensation and urban congestion in Dar es Salaam, drawing particularly on the experience of Kurasini, the Chamazi community-led resettlement response, recent concerns surrounding ICD expansion, and evidence from the Msimbazi flood-risk project. The analysis argues that the central problem is not simply displacement without compensation but development without distribution. Compensation systems centred principally on recognised property interests can leave tenants and economically dependent residents without adequate assistance to reconstruct their livelihoods. At the same time, the conversion of residential land into logistics infrastructure can create substantial future economic value from which displaced communities have no continuing claim. The article further argues that the proliferation of ICDs within the metropolitan area risks transferring the congestion problem from the port to surrounding communities unless logistics planning is integrated with land-use and rail infrastructure. The appropriate policy response is therefore not to reject port expansion, but to redesign its distributional architecture so that affected populations participate in compensation, resettlement, employment, value creation and the longer-term development dividend.

articles_hidden.title: Emotional Intelligence and Money Anxiety:  “An Empirical Study on Financial Stress Coping Mechanisms Among  Generation Z
articles_hidden.authors: Deepika Rathi; Jainish Bhagat; RONAK AJAYKUMAR MEHTA; Komal Sharma
articles_hidden.abstract:
Generation Z has entered adulthood under a distinctive combination of economic precarity, 
digital financial exposure, and social-media-amplified comparison, making financial stress a 
defining feature of their early financial socialisation. While emotional intelligence (EI) is well 
established in organisational and educational psychology as a predictor of stress regulation, 
its role in shaping how young adults respond to money-related anxiety remains 
underexamined in the financial-behaviour literature. This paper develops and specifies a 
structural model linking Emotional Intelligence, Money (Financial) Anxiety, and Coping 
Mechanisms among Generation Z, incorporating Financial Self-Efficacy as a boundary 
condition and Financial Literacy as a control variable. Drawing on the ability model of 
emotional intelligence (Salovey & Mayer, 1990), the transactional model of stress and coping 
(Lazarus & Folkman, 1984), and the financial-anxiety literature (Archuleta et al., 2013), 
seven hypotheses are proposed and a measurement model is specified using established, 
validated scales — the Schutte Self-Report Emotional Intelligence Test (Schutte et al., 1998), 
the Financial Anxiety Scale (Archuleta et al., 2011), and the Brief COPE (Carver, 1997). A 
Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) approach is proposed as the 
Page 1 of 23 
analytical strategy, given its suitability for exploratory, prediction-oriented models with 
formative and reflective constructs. The paper details the full measurement instrument, 
sampling strategy, and a step-by-step PLS-SEM assessment protocol (measurement model 
validity, structural model evaluation, mediation and moderation testing, and PLS predict) so 
that the study can proceed directly to data collection and empirical estimation. [Once data 
collection is complete, this abstract should be revised to state the actual sample size, key 
path coefficients, and principal findings.]

articles_hidden.title: Automated Suspicion: Algorithmic Workforce Surveillance and the Erosion of Internal Legitimacy in the Metropolitan Police Service
articles_hidden.authors: Paul Ford
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
This article examines the Metropolitan Police Service (MPS) pilot deployment of Palantir analytics for internal workforce monitoring, announced in April 2026 as part of the force’s post-Panorama standards programme. The force defends the deployment as lawful, since it brings together data it already holds; this article argues that defence repeats a known mistake in policing legitimacy research, treating legal compliance as the ceiling of consent rather than its floor. Drawing on procedural justice theory (Tyler 2006), the dialogic and twin-track models of legitimacy (Bottoms and Tankebe 2012; Tankebe 2013; Bradford and Tankebe 2014), Beetham’s (1991) account of institutional legitimacy, and the author’s earlier work (Ford 2021, 2026), it audits the deployment against the four pillars of procedural justice and finds it deficient on voice, neutrality, respect, and trustworthy motives. It argues that the pilot inverts Sherman’s (2007) power-few hypothesis, fails the targeting—testing—tracking discipline of evidence-based policing (Sherman 2013), substitutes a technical fix for what Heifetz (1994) calls an adaptive challenge, and entangles culture reform with surveillance in ways that risk delegitimising Equality, Diversity, and Inclusion (EDI) work and, through a mirroring effect, damaging public-facing encounters. A subsequent disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act 2000, including the pilot’s Data Protection Impact Assessment and Equality Impact Assessment obtained in redacted form, tests these claims against primary evidence: it confirms an algorithmic yield of 2.6 million flags with a further-action rate of 0.075 per cent, corroborates self-acknowledged risks to trust and equity in the MPS’s own equalities analysis, and shows the force cannot establish what became of the cases its own system flagged. The article closes with implications for chief officers, police and crime commissioners, and professional standards leads.
Keywords: algorithmic management, workforce surveillance, police legitimacy, officer self-legitimacy, procedural justice, psychological safety, organisational culture, EDI, Palantir, Metropolitan Police Service.

articles_hidden.title: Towards Developing Indicators of Environmental Sustainability for Kathmandu, Nepal
articles_hidden.authors: Ambika P. Adhikari
articles_hidden.abstract: Sustainability is now considered one of the key objectives in urban planning. However, due to inappropriate planning, weak institutions, limitation of resources, and poor implementation of policies, many big cities in developing countries have become even less environmentally, economically, and socially sustainable than they were in the past. Historically, the Kathmandu Valley enjoyed a unique tradition, rich heritage and a moderate state of sustainability in all areas, particularly in the environmental arena. However, the rapidly expanding and modernizing cities in the valley are facing serious problems of sustainability on all fronts: economic, social, environmental, and ecological. Whereas, environmental and economic sustainability were tacitly embedded in the traditional planning practices in Nepal, the rapid growth and modernization of the major cities in the valley are making them increasingly unsustainable. This paper proposes major indicators of sustainability and discusses an approach to implement sustainable practices in urban planning and development in Kathmandu.

articles_hidden.title: Rol de la Iglesia católica como aparato ideológico durante la dictadura de Trujillo, 1930-1961
articles_hidden.authors: Alfredo Antonio Perez Sanchez
articles_hidden.abstract:
La presente investigación analiza el rol de la Iglesia católica como aparato ideológico durante la dictadura de Trujillo, 1930-1961. El estudio parte del interés por comprender la relación establecida entre la Iglesia y el Estado, así como la influencia que dicha vinculación ejerció en la legitimación del régimen y en la difusión de valores, prácticas y discursos orientados a fortalecer el poder político durante la Era de Trujillo. La investigación se desarrolló desde un enfoque cualitativo, mediante un estudio histórico-documental sustentado en el análisis crítico de documentos oficiales, legislación, publicaciones periódicas, correspondencia, obras historiográficas y otras fuentes primarias y secundarias relacionadas con el tema. El análisis realizado permitió establecer que la Iglesia católica ocupó un lugar importante dentro de la estructura ideológica del régimen, al ejercer una influencia significativa en los ámbitos educativo, moral y simbólico de la sociedad dominicana. Además, se observó que esta relación no permaneció estática, ya que en los años finales de la dictadura comenzaron a manifestarse diferencias entre la jerarquía eclesiástica y el poder político, motivadas por el incremento de la represión y el deterioro de la situación nacional. En ese sentido, la investigación ofrece una interpretación histórica que amplía la comprensión de las relaciones entre religión, poder e ideología durante el trujillato y aporta una visión integral sobre este proceso de la historia dominicana.

Palabras clave: Iglesia católica; dictadura de Trujillo; aparato ideológico del Estado; legitimación política; ideología.

articles_hidden.title: Co-creating change in agriculture and food systems: A systematic review of co-creation processes and approaches for evaluating their contributions to sustainability transformation
articles_hidden.authors: Sara Delaney; Sophia Alami; Maria Busse; Bonnie Averbuch; Fanny Boeraeve; Pauline Cassart; Valéria Csonka; Graeme Dean; Cedric Gossart; Bienvenu Kambashi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Co-creation is widely proposed to address complex sustainability challenges by bringing together diverse forms of experience and expertise. Yet practical, evidence-based guidance on how co-creation processes can support sustainability transformation remains fragmented and insufficient, including for agriculture and food systems. We conducted a systematic literature review to characterize scholarly work on co-creation for environmental sustainability and to identify process insights relevant to Living Labs and related participatory initiatives. Following a four-stage screening procedure, we reviewed 5,291 articles and retained 266 studies describing multi-stakeholder, action-oriented, experimental processes; 51 agriculture- and food-focused articles were subjected to in-depth qualitative analysis. We combined bibliometric and descriptive analyses, including co-authorship network mapping, with framework-guided qualitative coding of co-creation inputs, processes, outcomes, impacts, and evaluation practices.
Publications on this topic increased substantially over the past decade, but relatively few studies documented action and experimentation in sufficient methodological detail. Agriculture and food studies constituted a moderately self-contained segment of the broader literature. Across the qualitative sample, five enabling factors were most consistently associated with productive co-creation: participant alignment, institutional support, strong facilitation, inclusive participation and trust, and sufficient time for iteration. Studies also identified recurring trade-offs between diversity and alignment, resource-intensive engagement and scalability, and place specificity and transferability. Frequently reported outcomes were new knowledge, communication and networks, empowerment or efficacy, and skills. However, evidence of longer-term sustainability impacts was limited: most articles described intermediate outcomes rather than demonstrated transformation. Only sixteen articles evaluated the co-creation process itself, and participatory development of evaluation criteria was rare. Co-creation efforts can build the practical and relational capacities, and “social infrastructure” needed for sustainability transitions, but stronger methodological reporting and participatory, longitudinal evaluation are needed for validation of criteria and proxies for impact and establishment of how these processes contribute to lasting transformation.

articles_hidden.title: The Illusion of Precision: Interpreting International Rankings Within Their Measurement Limits
articles_hidden.authors: Milos Kankaras
articles_hidden.abstract: International rankings publish precise country positions. We ask which comparisons the evidence behind five of them supports, by reproducing published tables, optimising weights, applying multiplicity-adjusted rank inference and two source checks, within a framework separating invalid measurement, insufficient validation, normative trade-offs, underrepresentation of uncertainty and misleading communication. In every programme the adjacent ordering is unsupported, each for a different reason: Report Card 19 trades off dimensions in all 35 adjacent pairs; World Happiness Report countries move a median of 30 places when affect replaces life evaluation; 23 of 38 countries can lead the Better Life Index under unrestricted weights; retrospective rescoring moves Global Health Security Index countries a median of seven places within one year; only 4 of 80 adjacent PISA pairs are distinguishable. Broad contrasts survive throughout. Two unrepresented uncertainties are documented: rotated administration behind Report Card 19's social-skills indicator, and unlinked assessment vintages behind the Human Capital Index.

articles_hidden.title: Are stereotypes of warmth and competence intersectionally complex? Investigating intersections of gender, sexuality, ethnicity, and religion.
articles_hidden.authors: Ely Strömberg; Valentina Di Stasio; Jeremy Michael Jesse Kuhnle; Vasilena Lachkovska; Bram Lancee; Stefanie L. Sprong; Stephanie Steinmetz; Sanne van Oosten; Susanne Veit; Elli Zey
articles_hidden.abstract:
Intersectional stereotype research has consistently found that stereotypes vary simultaneously
across categories such as race and gender. Recently, studies have started to investigate the
complex interplay of multiple (more than two) categories, with some finding that stereotypes
are best viewed as based on independent categories. By contrast, other studies find that
stereotypes are intersectionally complex, meaning that they result from unique combinations
of categories. We fielded a harmonized factorial survey experiment across nine European
countries (n = 20,339) in which respondents evaluated perceived warmth and competence of
vignette profiles that varied on gender, sexuality, ethnicity, and religion. We find that while
main effects account for 95% of stereotype variance, compared with 5% of interactions,
single category stereotypes still show effect variation; sometimes to the degree that a negative
stereotype turns positive. Our study shows that stereotypes are primarily explained by
categorical effects, but with small but consistent intersectional effects.
